 [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1936.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1936.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Time_do_São_Paulo,_1936.tif)

São Paulo team in 1936.

The club had intended to debut in 1935, but due to the merger and disaffiliation from APEA, this was not possible. Thus, the new club's debut was scheduled for January 25, 1936, against [Portuguesa Santista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associação_Atlética_Portuguesa_(Santos) "Associação Atlética Portuguesa (Santos)"), at the [Estádio Antônio Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Antarctica_Paulista "Estádio Antarctica Paulista"). On the same day, a celebration for the city's anniversary was taking place on [Paulista Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulista_Avenue "Paulista Avenue"), and a decree from the Education Secretariat prohibited events that could rival the parade. With little time before the match, Porfírio went to Paulista Avenue to persuade Dr. Cantídio Campos, then municipal education secretary, to authorize the game. Porfírio took the stage and argued in favor of the team bearing the city's name and colors. Cantídio accepted the arguments and authorized the opening of the gates and the match. However, at the time of heading to the stadium, no trams were running in the city. Once again, Porfírio rented cars with his own money to transport players and fans to the match.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

In its early years of this new phase, the club was known by other teams and their fans as a team of "paupers." Furthermore, the press generally referred to the club as "poor," calling it "Júnior," "Club No. 2," and "São-Paulinho." In the view of much of the São Paulo population, the new entity could not achieve the glories of its predecessor or reach the same level as [Corinthians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_Club_Corinthians_Paulista "Sport Club Corinthians Paulista") and [Palestra Itália](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SE_Palmeiras "SE Palmeiras").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) However, after so many obstacles and resurgences, it earned the nickname "Club of Faith" in 1937, coined by journalist Tomás Mazzoni, a moniker that endures to this day.[[1]](#cite_note-siteoficial_origens-1)[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[13]](#cite_note-revoficial_133a-13)

> Recently, São Paulo FC Júnior emerged with the same ambitions as its predecessor. If the new São Paulo came into the world of football without the assets, fame, and prestige of its ancestors, it brought the greatest wealth: faith in its destiny and love for its present. Only faith could lead the current Tricolor to be born like any neighborhood club and quickly become an organization on the right path to progress in top-tier football. The Club of Faith, as the current São Paulo FC deserves to be called (...)

— **Tomás Mazzoni**, [[13]](#cite_note-revoficial_133a-13)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Igreja_da_Consola%C3%A7%C3%A3o%2C_SP%2C_torre.JPG/250px-Igreja_da_Consola%C3%A7%C3%A3o%2C_SP%2C_torre.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Igreja_da_Consolação,_SP,_torre.JPG)

Tower of the Consolação Church, where half the team stayed.

At that time, the club had no members, revenue sources, or even assets. It trained and played wherever it was allowed. There was no place for team lodging, which had to be improvised, with half the squad staying at the home of president Frederico Menzen and the other half in bunk beds in the tower of the [Consolação Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igreja_Nossa_Senhora_da_Consolação_(São_Paulo) "Igreja Nossa Senhora da Consolação (São Paulo)"), the parish of Monsignor Bastos, a notable São Paulo supporter. Training sessions were sometimes held in the church's courtyard alongside the area where the [Sodality of Our Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodality_of_Our_Lady "Sodality of Our Lady") played [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"). When available, the team trained at the Várzea do Glicério field, but with the condition of vacating the premises as soon as the field's owning teams arrived.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/SPFC_squad_-_1938_-_01.jpg/250px-SPFC_squad_-_1938_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPFC_squad_-_1938_-_01.jpg)

São Paulo team in 1938.

However, despite the determination and faith of its directors and the strong popular appeal inherited from Paulistano and Palmeiras, the São Paulo players, with rare exceptions, were technically weak. The team achieved only an eighth-place finish in the [1936 Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Campeonato_Paulista "1936 Campeonato Paulista") and a seventh-place finish in the [following year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1937_Campeonato_Paulista "1937 Campeonato Paulista").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) This would be addressed with a new merger: in 1938, the Clube Atlético Estudante Paulista, founded in May 1935 by São Paulo dissidents, went on a tour to [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile") and [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"), during which the manager absconded with the collected funds, leaving the club on the brink of bankruptcy. São Paulo, aware of the situation, proposed a merger, as Estudante had talented players and owned the [Estádio Antônio Alonso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Antarctica_Paulista "Estádio Antarctica Paulista"); São Paulo, on the other hand, had a fanbase, charisma, and balanced finances. The question of the club's name arose. The tricolors argued that they were older, had an established tradition, and carried the name and colors of the state. These arguments prevailed, on the condition that the new president be a neutral figure connected to both clubs, Piragibe Nogueira. Another decision was that members of both clubs would have their membership numbers reset to facilitate the merger. São Paulo then raised the funds to settle the debt, and the agreement was finalized. On August 25, 1938, the new team debuted, already featuring half of Estudante’s players, including [Roberto Gomes Pedrosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Gomes_Pedrosa "Roberto Gomes Pedrosa"), a future club president. The new headquarters was established at Dom José de Barros Street, number 337, in [República](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/República_(district_of_São_Paulo) "República (district of São Paulo)").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/SPFC_squad_-_1939_-_01.jpg/250px-SPFC_squad_-_1939_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPFC_squad_-_1939_-_01.jpg)

Photo of the tricolor squad after finishing as runner-up in the 1938 championship.

Weeks before the merger, on July 3, 1938, São Paulo held the "São Paulo FC Festival," offering the Henrique Mündel Trophy to the winner to raise funds, despite the club’s finances already being stabilized.[[14]](#cite_note-folhamanha_interessantefestival-14)

After the merger, with a capable team, the tricolor reached the runner-up position in the [1938 Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_Campeonato_Paulista "1938 Campeonato Paulista")—it could have been champion if not for a controversial handball goal by Corinthians’ forward Carlinhos, validated by the referee (the draw gave the title to Corinthians).[[15]](#cite_note-unzelte_almanaquecor-15) In 1939, the players were still adjusting, finishing only fifth in the [Paulista Championship that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_Campeonato_Paulista "1939 Campeonato Paulista").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) During this period, the club began to encourage the practice of sports other than football.[[16]](#cite_note-siteoficial_ospfc-16)

São Paulo was a pioneer in [organized supporter groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torcida_organizada "Torcida organizada"). In 1939, a student, [Manoel Raymundo Paes de Almeida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manoel_Raymundo_Paes_de_Almeida "Manoel Raymundo Paes de Almeida"), founded the Grêmio São-Paulino in [Mooca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mooca_(district_of_São_Paulo) "Mooca (district of São Paulo)"), which later became TUSP—*Torcida Uniformizada do São Paulo*. It was an enthusiastic supporter group that held its own celebrations with streamers and confetti.[[17]](#cite_note-loyola_saga-17)

## 1940 to 1949

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1940 to 1949")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/Pacaembu3.jpg/250px-Pacaembu3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pacaembu3.jpg)

Pacaembu Stadium, where the club earned the nickname "The Most Beloved."

After April 27, 1940, with the inauguration of the [Pacaembu Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacaembu_Stadium "Pacaembu Stadium"), Paulista football was never the same. From that date, the city boasted what was then the largest and most modern stadium in [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America"), with a capacity for seventy thousand fans. This shifted the epicenter of football from [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro") to São Paulo, making it not only a sporting event but a social one as well. It was during the [Vargas dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vargas_era "Vargas era"), when displays of state flags were prohibited.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[18]](#cite_note-constituicao_1937-18)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Cartaz_Revolucion%C3%A1rio_1.jpg/250px-Cartaz_Revolucion%C3%A1rio_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cartaz_Revolucionário_1.jpg)

Paulista poster against the dictatorship.

People began arriving early, around 10:00 a.m., and at the time of the festivities, it is estimated that the crowd was between sixty thousand and eighty thousand. Many authorities were present in the honorary stands, including [Getúlio Vargas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getúlio_Vargas "Getúlio Vargas"), the president of the Republic, who was not particularly admired by Paulistas. The festivities began with a parade of delegations from [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), [Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay "Uruguay"), Peru, [Paraná](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraná_(state) "Paraná (state)"), [Minas Gerais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minas_Gerais "Minas Gerais"), Rio de Janeiro, the interior of [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo_(state) "São Paulo (state)"), and the city clubs. The Corinthians and Palestra Itália teams were the first to enter, receiving enthusiastic applause, but nothing compared to the entrance of the *Tricolor Paulista*. The entire stadium and radio broadcasters, outraged by the censorship, circumvented it by standing to applaud the tricolor delegation—which carried the name and colors of the Paulista flag—as a response to the president, who had been unpopular in São Paulo since the [1932 Constitutionalist Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutionalist_Revolution "Constitutionalist Revolution"). The crowd stood to salute the delegation and, pointing to the stand where Getúlio Vargas was, shouted the team’s name.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

> The sporting public itself demonstrated how beloved São Paulo FC is, as, despite presenting a small group, it received warm applause, with its name deliberately cheered.

— **[Folha da Manhã](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grupo_Folha "Grupo Folha")**, [[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The next day, the newspaper *A Gazeta Esportiva* featured the headline "The Most Beloved Club in the City" on its front page. Some time later, the DEIP—State Department of Press and Propaganda—held a public contest among fans of all the era’s clubs to determine which was truly the most beloved by the city’s citizens. With Corinthians and Palestra Itália as favorites—having the largest fanbases—the winner was São Paulo, with 5,523 votes, more than the combined votes of its two main competitors: 2,671 for Corinthians and 2,593 for Palestra. Thus, São Paulo officially became "The Most Beloved," a slogan that the club still uses today.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

In the same year, on May 19, São Paulo won the first official title at Pacaembu, the Torneio Início of the Paulista Championship, against archrival Corinthians.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) However, in the tournament for the state trophy, it finished only sixth. In 1941, the team reached the [state championship runner-up position](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1941_Campeonato_Paulista "1941 Campeonato Paulista"), once again contending for the title.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Le%C3%B4nidas_da_Silva_and_Arthur_Friedenreich_01.jpg/250px-Le%C3%B4nidas_da_Silva_and_Arthur_Friedenreich_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Leônidas_da_Silva_and_Arthur_Friedenreich_01.jpg)

Leônidas da Silva alongside another tricolor idol, [Friedenreich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Friedenreich "Arthur Friedenreich").

In 1942, São Paulo would experience a turning point in its history with [Leônidas da Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leônidas_da_Silva "Leônidas da Silva"). Already with some national fame, he played a match in December 1932 for the [Brazilian national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team") against the [Uruguay team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay_national_football_team "Uruguay national football team"), scoring both goals in a 2–1 victory. For his performance, he earned the nickname "Black Diamond." His other nickname, "Rubber Man," came from his performance against [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia_national_football_team "Czechoslovakia national football team"), where, in addition to scoring two goals, he executed his most famous move, the bicycle kick. Leônidas debuted on May 24, 1942, against Corinthians and ended the championship elevating the team to third place, with hopes of a promising future.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Leônidas was a turning point in São Paulo's history, as the club had only won one state championship, in 1931, and from the moment he debuted, São Paulo amassed several titles.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Due to the large crowd (70,281 people, the all-time Pacaembu attendance record) and the significance of this debut match, the classic between the *Tricolor* and the *Alvinegro Paulista* became known as [*Majestoso*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clássico_Majestoso "Clássico Majestoso"), a nickname given by *A Gazeta Esportiva* journalist Tomás Mazzoni.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Antonio_Sastre.jpg/250px-Antonio_Sastre.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antonio_Sastre.jpg)

[Antonio Sastre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Sastre "Antonio Sastre"), an Argentine player who was part of the tricolor squad from 1943 to 1946.

In that same year, Brazil was going through a delicate historical moment. Amid [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), anti-Italian sentiment flared in the country due to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")’s alignment with the [Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers"). In this context, the government imposed harsh repression on countries opposing the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[19]](#cite_note-decreto-lei_4166_1942-19)[[20]](#cite_note-decreto-lei_4806_1942-20) As a result, [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") and Italian institutions were closed, renamed, or directly intervened by the government. Among the clubs, [Cruzeiro Esporte Clube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruzeiro_Esporte_Clube "Cruzeiro Esporte Clube"), also called Palestra Itália, changed its name. The green-and-whites, however, believe the persecution was instigated by São Paulo, which was allegedly interested in taking over the [Estádio Palestra Itália](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Palestra_Itália "Estádio Palestra Itália"). [Oberdan Cattani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberdan_Cattani "Oberdan Cattani"), Palestra’s goalkeeper, once claimed that São Paulo controlled the Paulista Federation and acted accordingly. However, the *Tricolor Paulista* was still a lesser team at the time and Getúlio Vargas held little sympathy for the club after the events at Pacaembu’s inauguration.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) In the same year, São Paulo partnered with the Deutsch Sportive—which also faced prejudice due to its German origin—and gained a training field, the [Canindé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_do_Canindé "Estádio do Canindé").[[21]](#cite_note-guedes_imigrantes-21) Although it was a partnership, the Canindé land—equivalent to seventy thousand [square meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_meter "Square meter")—was purchased for the equivalent of 740 *[contos de réis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_real_(old) "Brazilian real (old)")*. São Paulo would become known as the *Canindé Tricolor*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

At the meeting to set the [1943 Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1943_Campeonato_Paulista "1943 Campeonato Paulista") calendar at the [Paulista Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federação_Paulista_de_Futebol "Federação Paulista de Futebol") headquarters, a Corinthians director remarked that the meeting was unnecessary, as tossing a coin would determine the champion: heads for Corinthians, tails for Palmeiras—formerly Palestra Itália. When questioned about São Paulo by the tricolor representative, the director replied that if the coin landed on its edge, São Paulo would be the champion—and if it stayed in the air, Portuguesa.[[22]](#cite_note-revoficial_75a-22) Until that moment, the Tricolor was seen as a mid-tier team that did not rival the aforementioned competitors. Thus began the championship, with São Paulo determined to break the hegemony of Corinthians and Palmeiras. In the final match, against Palmeiras, São Paulo held a goalless draw and clinched the title: the coin landed on its edge.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Following this achievement, the Grêmio São-Paulino held a nighttime parade with a float featuring a coin standing on its edge to collect the Taça dos Invictos at the *A Gazeta Esportiva* building.[[17]](#cite_note-loyola_saga-17)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1949.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1949.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Time_do_São_Paulo,_1949.tif)

São Paulo team, 1949. [National Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_of_Brazil "National Archives of Brazil").

The 1940s were the most successful decade for the tricolor in terms of titles up to that point: five titles, including two back-to-back championships—[1945 Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1945_Campeonato_Paulista "1945 Campeonato Paulista")/[1946 Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Campeonato_Paulista "1946 Campeonato Paulista") and [1948 Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Campeonato_Paulista "1948 Campeonato Paulista")/[1949 Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Campeonato_Paulista "1949 Campeonato Paulista")—and an unbeaten title in 1946.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) This team became known as the "Steamroller"—when it took the field, only the score was unknown, as victory was assured—and it helped establish São Paulo as a sports association, as the club rapidly developed numerous activities from this period onward.[[23]](#cite_note-revoficial_81a-23)

With São Paulo’s hegemony, coupled with the accusation regarding the takeover of Palestra Itália and the title disputes between the clubs, the classic gained significance and was nicknamed, once again by Tomás Mazzoni, the *[Choque-Rei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choque-Rei "Choque-Rei")*.[[24]](#cite_note-24) It was also from this decade that the club, alongside Corinthians and Palmeiras, formed the so-called *Trio de Ferro*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

During this period, departments for [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics"), [fencing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fencing "Fencing"), [boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing "Boxing"), [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball "Volleyball"), and [chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") were created, all in 1943.,[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10) as well as basketball.[[25]](#cite_note-tricolormania_basquete-25) Some of these, however, were not very successful and closed after a few years, such as fencing, chess, and volleyball, with the latter resuming activities in the mid-1970s.[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10) Among the many departments created, athletics stands out, as in its second year, 1944, it won a series of fourteen Paulista titles, which continued until 1957. From 1961, it would reclaim these titles until 1966, totaling twenty championships in 25 years.[[26]](#cite_note-siteoficial_atletismo-26)

## 1950 to 1959

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1950 to 1959")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/N%C3%ADlton_De_Sordi_01.jpg/250px-N%C3%ADlton_De_Sordi_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nílton_De_Sordi_01.jpg)

[De Sordi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nílton_de_Sordi "Nílton de Sordi") honored for the 50th anniversary of the 1958 World Cup victory.

The 1950s began with high expectations for the team that had dominated the previous decade.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Additionally, on January 4, 1950, Leônidas scored his last goal for the club and retired after three more matches on January 21. The team's performance in the absence of its star player was a subject of keen interest.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) At the end of the previous decade, a movement to build a stadium worthy of the club’s achievements gained momentum. The then-president [Cícero Pompeu de Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cícero_Pompeu_de_Toledo "Cícero Pompeu de Toledo") led the group in favor of the stadium, arguing that the club could not only win titles but also needed to grow its assets.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Many, including some within the club, opposed the construction, arguing it was a risky endeavor that could severely harm the club’s finances, as the project aimed not just to build a large stadium but the largest private stadium in the world.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

> Do the difficult now and the impossible a little later.

— **[Cícero Pompeu de Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cícero_Pompeu_de_Toledo "Cícero Pompeu de Toledo")**, [[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27)

The original idea was to build the stadium on the Canindé land itself, but with the construction of the [Marginal Tietê](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marginal_Tietê "Marginal Tietê"), two-thirds of the land—about 20,000 square meters—were expropriated by the city hall, and building a stadium there was ruled out.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27) With this initial setback, Luís Campos Aranha told Pompeu de Toledo that he knew someone who could reorganize the club to make the stadium possible. That person was [Laudo Natel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laudo_Natel "Laudo Natel"), financial director of [Bradesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradesco "Bradesco") and a São Paulo supporter.[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10) To secure a bank loan, São Paulo needed to settle its debts.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27) To this end, Natel suggested selling the club’s only asset, the Canindé. The training field was sold to Wadih Sadi, a club counselor,[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) with the condition that the club could continue training there until another location was found.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27)

> We cannot be a club of eleven shirts, one flag, and many debts haunting us.

— **[Laudo Natel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laudo_Natel "Laudo Natel")**, [[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e7/Dino_Sani_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dino_Sani_01.jpg)

[Dino Sani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dino_Sani "Dino Sani"), one of the heroes of the 1958 World Cup victory, played for the club from 1954 to 1961.

With the debts cleared and the loan secured, the club sought a location that met the requirements, quickly selecting a flooded terrain in the [Ibirapuera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibirapuera "Ibirapuera") neighborhood, where the [Ibirapuera Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parque_Ibirapuera "Parque Ibirapuera") now stands. Mayor Armando de Arruda Pereira approved the use of the land and sent a proposal to the City Council for official approval. However, [Jnio Quadros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jnio_Quadros "Jnio Quadros"), president of the council, opposed and vetoed the project.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) The solution was to build the stadium far from the [city center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Zone_of_São_Paulo "Central Zone of São Paulo"), in an area then known as Jardim Leonor, which later became the [Morumbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morumbi,_São_Paulo "Morumbi, São Paulo") neighborhood.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) The area, uninhabited and lacking infrastructure, was being subdivided by the Aricanduva real estate company, and in December 1951, São Paulo, through Luís Aranha, secured a donation of land originally intended for parks and gardens.[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10) The donation was formalized on August 4, 1952, in exchange for the purchase of part of the land.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27) The city hall mediated the process and imposed certain construction conditions.[[28]](#cite_note-escritura_doacao-28) On August 15, the cornerstone was blessed by Monsignor Bastos, and the deed of possession was signed by Pompeu de Toledo. On the same day, a pro-stadium committee, chaired by Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, was formed, independent of the club’s board and dedicated solely to the stadium.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Even before the project was chosen, season tickets were already being sold by goalkeeper [José Poy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Poy "José Poy") of his own initiative, as the board only intended to use his image. Poy was highly successful, selling 8,000 of the 12,000 season tickets available.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Many projects were submitted to the committee, including one from a Soviet construction company, Antonov & Solnnerkevic, which proposed a transparent and removable roof for the entire stadium. However, the chosen project was that of [João Batista Vilanova Artigas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/João_Batista_Vilanova_Artigas "João Batista Vilanova Artigas"), a renowned architect from the Paulista School, mainly due to its capacity for 150,000 people. Construction began in 1953, with land stabilization, gallery construction, and field drainage.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The stadium’s name was yet to be decided: "9 de Julho," in homage to the 1932 Constitutionalist Revolution, and even "Paulistão" were considered, but in 1957, Cícero Pompeu de Toledo fell ill and stepped down. Sensing he would not live much longer, councilors gathered signatures to name the stadium after its visionary and greatest advocate, [Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Cícero_Pompeu_de_Toledo "Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) In 1958, Cícero died, but he knew his dream would come to fruition.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27) With his death, a new committee was formed, this time led by Laudo Natel.[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10) Construction proceeded firmly, overcoming immense challenges, as no public funds were provided for the project.[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10)

From 1952 to 1959, the club allocated all its funds to the stadium but still managed to field competitive teams with star players, winning the Paulista Championships of [1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_Campeonato_Paulista "1953 Campeonato Paulista") and [1957](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1957_Campeonato_Paulista "1957 Campeonato Paulista"),[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) the latter marking the farewell of [Teixeirinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teixeirinha_(footballer,_born_1922) "Teixeirinha (footballer, born 1922)") and featuring the experience of Rio native [Zizinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zizinho "Zizinho"), then 35 years old, on the field and Hungarian coach [Béla Guttmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Béla_Guttmann "Béla Guttmann") on the bench.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

The 1953 Paulista Championship earned the club the title of "IV Centenary Champion" of the city of São Paulo,[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) as the title was only decided on January 24, 1954,[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) one day before the city’s 400th anniversary, making the team the legitimate Paulista champion of the anniversary celebrations.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

São Paulo also finished as runner-up in the Paulista Championships of [1950](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1950_Campeonato_Paulista "1950 Campeonato Paulista"), [1952](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Campeonato_Paulista "1952 Campeonato Paulista"), 1956, and 1958.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) Starting with the 1956 championship, lost to Santos, the classic between the two teams was nicknamed *[San-São](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San–São "San–São")* by journalist Tommaso Mazzoni.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The year 1952 was also fruitful for the club’s athletics, specifically in the [triple jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_jump "Triple jump") event, as [Adhemar Ferreira da Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adhemar_Ferreira_da_Silva "Adhemar Ferreira da Silva"), an athlete developed by the club in 1947, set the world record in the category at the [1952 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"), a feat repeated at the [1955 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1955_Pan_American_Games "1955 Pan American Games") in [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico").[[10]](#cite_note-grandesclubes_2_spfc-10)[[26]](#cite_note-siteoficial_atletismo-26) These two records and their respective achievements were immortalized in the club’s crest with two gold stars in 1955 and later on the uniform in 1997.[[29]](#cite_note-siteoficial_simbolos-29)

## 1960 to 1969

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1960 to 1969")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Hilderaldo_Bellini.jpg/250px-Hilderaldo_Bellini.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hilderaldo_Bellini.jpg)

[Bellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilderaldo_Bellini "Hilderaldo Bellini"), captain of the 1958 World Cup team, played for São Paulo in the 1960s.

The 1960s were marked by the dominance of [Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santos_FC "Santos FC") led by [Pelé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelé "Pelé"), which won nearly every competition it entered. Compounding the issue was the unresolved situation regarding the completion of São Paulo's stadium.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The club lacked the funds to complete the construction, and one solution was to inaugurate the stadium before it was fully finished to generate revenue from ticket sales and rentals to other clubs.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Thus, on October 2, 1960, in front of 64,748 spectators, the Cícero Pompeu de Toledo Stadium was inaugurated with a match against [Sporting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporting_CP "Sporting CP") from [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal").[[30]](#cite_note-revoficial_106a-30)

With the stadium now able to host matches, the club sought new ways to raise funds for its completion. One method was the *Carnê Paulistão*, a type of lottery created by television presenter and club supporter Hélio Setti from [Rede Excelsior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rede_Excelsior "Rede Excelsior"). It awarded prizes on television to those who kept up with their ticket payments, similar to the current *Baú da Felicidade*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Other sources of funding included partnerships, commercial exchanges,[[31]](#cite_note-ET_inauguracaomorumbi-31) and financial loans,[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27) as well as the sale of patrimonial and social memberships, which helped raise funds for both the stadium's completion and the development of the club's social facilities.[[32]](#cite_note-revoficial_108a-32) Toward the end of the construction, the city government proposed exchanging the new stadium for the Pacaembu Stadium, to which Laudo Natel promptly replied that "the São Paulo fan's dream does not fit in Pacaembu."[[31]](#cite_note-ET_inauguracaomorumbi-31)

Due to the stadium's construction, the club experienced its longest title drought between 1957 and 1970, totaling thirteen years without major titles. During this period, the club won the [Rio-São Paulo Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio-São_Paulo_Tournament "Rio-São Paulo Tournament") in 1958, the Pentagonal de Guadalajara ([Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico")) in 1960, the Quadrangular de Cali ([Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia")) in 1960, the São Paulo Second Division Championship in 1960 and 1962, the [Small World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Club_World_Cup "Small Club World Cup") ([Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela")) in 1963, the Triangular Tournament of El Salvador ([El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador")) in 1964, the Florence Tournament ([Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")) in 1964, and the Colombino Huelva Trophy ([Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")) in 1969, totaling nine titles. Even so, this title drought was the shortest among its state rivals.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

While the football team struggled to win titles, the boxing section enjoyed its most successful period. Spanning the 1940s, 1950s, and 1960s, the golden era of boxing was anchored by the Zumbano/Jofre family boxing academy, where most athletes were trained by Aristides Kid Jofre, father of [Éder Jofre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Éder_Jofre "Éder Jofre"). During this time, the academy produced fighters who became famous and won Brazilian, South American, and world titles. In 1960, Éder Jofre won his first world title for São Paulo, the [World Boxing Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Boxing_Association "World Boxing Association") (WBA) Bantamweight title. Two years later, in 1962, he won the Unified Bantamweight World Championship.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

## 1970 to 1979

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1970 to 1979")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1971.tif/lossy-page1-250px-Time_do_S%C3%A3o_Paulo%2C_1971.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Time_do_São_Paulo,_1971.tif)

São Paulo team, 1971. [National Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archives_of_Brazil "National Archives of Brazil").

The largest private stadium in the world at the time was complete, allowing the club to refocus on its football team. As a result, they signed the [midfielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_midfielder "Defensive midfielder") [Édson Cegonha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Édson_Cegonha "Édson Cegonha"), the [center-forward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_(association_football) "Forward (association football)") [Toninho Guerreiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toninho_Guerreiro "Toninho Guerreiro"), the [right-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full-back_(association_football) "Full-back (association football)") [Pablo Forlán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Forlán "Pablo Forlán"), and the [midfielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder "Midfielder") [Gérson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gérson_de_Oliveira_Nunes "Gérson de Oliveira Nunes"), forming a very strong team,[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) although it would require until 1970 for the squad to reach its full potential and cohesion.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

Following these signings, the stadium was to be definitively inaugurated. On January 25, 1970, the final inauguration took place. However, days before the match, construction debris, including wood, remained on the field, and the company responsible for its removal quoted a 40-day timeline. A club director with contacts in the military learned they needed firewood and proposed that the club would donate the wood if the military could remove it in a single day. The deal was struck, and the wood was cleared.[[31]](#cite_note-ET_inauguracaomorumbi-31)

The scale of the stadium’s construction was impressive. It used fifty thousand [cubic meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_meter "Cubic meter") of concrete, four hundred thousand bags of cement, and six thousand tons of iron. The area designated for the public spanned 64,450 square meters.[[34]](#cite_note-revoficial_75b-34)

The match against [Porto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Porto "FC Porto") from [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal") was a turning point, as fans and directors pressed then-president Laudo Natel about the title drought. He consistently responded that having a team without assets was pointless and promised that once the stadium was built, he would assemble a competitive team to win a title within one or two years—a promise fulfilled in the year of the inauguration and repeated the following year.[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Cicero_pompeu_de_toledo_-_aerial_-_02.jpg/250px-Cicero_pompeu_de_toledo_-_aerial_-_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cicero_pompeu_de_toledo_-_aerial_-_02.jpg)

Aerial view of the Morumbi Stadium and part of its surrounding neighborhood.

The stadium also helped dispel claims that its location in the Morumbi neighborhood would remain undeveloped. The area, previously characterized by a state of complete absence of urban infrastructure, has undergone a substantial transformation, with the introduction of essential services such as sewage, water, and electricity. Presently, Morumbi is regarded as one of the most exclusive and sophisticated neighborhoods within the city, boasting some of the most exorbitant real estate prices in the capital on a per-square-meter basis. Due to its location, the stadium became known as Morumbi, and the team, previously called *São Paulo da Floresta* and *Tricolor do Canindé*, became the *Tricolor do Morumbi*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[27]](#cite_note-spnet_laudonatel-27)[[31]](#cite_note-ET_inauguracaomorumbi-31)

Thus, in the 1970s, São Paulo overcame challenges in various aspects. In 1971, it achieved a runner-up finish in the [Brazilian Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1971 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A")—its best result up to that point—and qualified for the [Libertadores of 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Copa_Libertadores "1972 Copa Libertadores"), finishing fourth. From the start of the decade, the club improved its performance, winning the São Paulo State Championships of [1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Campeonato_Paulista "1970 Campeonato Paulista"), [1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1971_Campeonato_Paulista "1971 Campeonato Paulista"), and [1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Campeonato_Paulista "1975 Campeonato Paulista"), as well as the unprecedented [Brazilian Championship of 1977](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1977_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1977 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"). There were also runner-up finishes in the [Brazilian Championship of 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1973 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") and the [Libertadores of 1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Copa_Libertadores "1974 Copa Libertadores").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Serginho_chulapa.jpg/250px-Serginho_chulapa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Serginho_chulapa.jpg)

Serginho Chulapa, the club’s all-time top scorer.

The first Brazilian Championship title was arguably the club’s most unlikely, as experts considered the team average and not among the favorites, despite having the country’s best coach, [Rubens Minelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubens_Minelli "Rubens Minelli"), and a squad with nine players who had played or would play for the [Brazil national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_football_team "Brazil national football team"). The team played the entire championship winning when it needed to and losing when it could afford to—suffering only two defeats in the first two phases—until reaching the decisive matches. In the third phase, they lost only to [Botafogo de Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botafogo_Futebol_Clube_(SP) "Botafogo Futebol Clube (SP)"), and even then, with a wrongly disallowed goal that led to the suspension of striker [Serginho Chulapa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serginho_Chulapa "Serginho Chulapa") after he kicked the assistant referee who had nullified the goal. In the semifinals, they overcame the tournament’s [dark horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_horse "Dark horse"), [Operário de Campo Grande](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operário_Futebol_Clube_(MS) "Operário Futebol Clube (MS)"), with a 3–0 home win and a 1–0 away loss.[[35]](#cite_note-35)

Thus, [Atlético Mineiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlético_Mineiro "Atlético Mineiro") and São Paulo reached the final, which was a single match at the [Governador Magalhães Pinto Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineirão "Mineirão"), with Atlético Mineiro favored to win. In the final, both teams were without their star players—Serginho for São Paulo and [Reinaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Reinaldo_de_Lima "José Reinaldo de Lima") for Atlético.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Following the coach’s orders, São Paulo employed tight marking, stifling Atlético’s play while creating the best scoring chances. The match went to extra time, but no goals were scored. In the penalty shootout, the key was the mind games of São Paulo’s goalkeeper [Waldir Peres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldir_Peres "Waldir Peres"), who unsettled Atlético’s penalty takers, leading to three misses and securing the title for the *Tricolor do Morumbi*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

However, in 1978, São Paulo failed to win the [Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Campeonato_Paulista "1978 Campeonato Paulista") against Santos, which was decided in mid-1979, and soon after, opted out of the [Brazilian Championship of 1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1979 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") to focus on the [Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Campeonato_Paulista "1979 Campeonato Paulista"), where it finished only seventh, signaling the need for change.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

[Éder Jofre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Éder_Jofre "Éder Jofre") had already achieved glory with two world titles, but two controversial points losses in 1965 and 1966 led him to retire from boxing. In 1969, Éder surprised everyone by returning to the ring, this time in the featherweight division. Despite moving up a weight class, he achieved an incredible streak of 25 victories, one of which earned him the [World Boxing Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Boxing_Council "World Boxing Council") (WBC) Featherweight World Championship title in 1973.[[36]](#cite_note-terra_atletasseculo-36)

## 1980 to 1989

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1980 to 1989")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Lu%C3%ADs_Ant%C3%B4nio_Corr%C3%AAa_da_Costa_%28M%C3%BCller%29_01.jpg/250px-Lu%C3%ADs_Ant%C3%B4nio_Corr%C3%AAa_da_Costa_%28M%C3%BCller%29_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Luís_Antônio_Corrêa_da_Costa_(Müller)_01.jpg)

The group known as the *Menudos do Morumbi* included Müller in its squad.

The year 1980 began with an unwanted record: Brazil had not won the [Saint Silvester Road Race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Silvester_Road_Race "Saint Silvester Road Race") in 34 years. São Paulo’s runner [José João da Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_João_da_Silva "José João da Silva") ended this drought, winning the title and setting Brazilian records for the 5,000 and 10,000 meters, which stood for sixteen years. In 1985, after undergoing knee surgery and breaking an arm, he won the race again, wearing the *Tricolor do Morumbi* colors.[[37]](#cite_note-saosilvestre_josejoao1985-37)[[38]](#cite_note-saosilvestre_historiainternac-38)

In football, the team started the 1980s strongly, winning back-to-back São Paulo State Championships in [1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Campeonato_Paulista "1980 Campeonato Paulista") and [1981](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Campeonato_Paulista "1981 Campeonato Paulista") and finishing as runner-up in the [Brazilian Championship of 1981](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1981 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), earning the nicknames *Máquina Tricolor* and *Tricolaço*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) Starting in 1981, the club engaged in a series of exchanges with [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") teams, beginning with [Cosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Cosmos_(1971–1985) "New York Cosmos (1971–1985)"), which brought defender [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Oscar_Bernardi "José Oscar Bernardi") to the club. Also in 1981, the club had the honor of playing with the number 10 [Rivellino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Rivellino "Roberto Rivellino") in a friendly against the [Saudi Arabian national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia_national_football_team "Saudi Arabia national football team").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) During this period, the club underwent a major overhaul of its board of directors, who began managing the club ambitiously with the goal of elevating it to European standards. To this end, several players, including Müller and [Chicão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicão_(footballer,_born_1949) "Chicão (footballer, born 1949)"), were gradually sold, while others, such as [Renato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Renato_Frederico "Carlos Renato Frederico") and [Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Oscar_Bernardi "José Oscar Bernardi"), were signed.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

> It’s more than *Tricolor*, it’s *Tricolor* with steel, it’s *Tricolaço*!

— **Team slogan inspired by a tire commercial**, [[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Antonio_de_Oliveira_Filho_%28Careca%29_01.jpg/250px-Antonio_de_Oliveira_Filho_%28Careca%29_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Antonio_de_Oliveira_Filho_(Careca)_01.jpg)

Careca, who scored the equalizing goal in the 1986 Brazilian Championship final.

The team started 1982 well, but a [runner-up finish in the Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Campeonato_Paulista "1982 Campeonato Paulista") lost to Corinthians signaled the start of a transitional phase. Serginho Chulapa transferred to Santos in 1983, and the board signed the young and talented [Careca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Careca "Careca") in his place, but the struggles continued with another [runner-up finish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Campeonato_Paulista "1983 Campeonato Paulista"), again to Corinthians. In 1984, coach [Cilinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otacílio_Pires_de_Camargo "Otacílio Pires de Camargo") began reshaping the team, and in the following year, he promoted several youth players, including [Müller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Antônio_Corrêa_da_Costa "Luís Antônio Corrêa da Costa") and [Silas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Silas_do_Prado_Pereira "Paulo Silas do Prado Pereira"). After a surprising comeback in a draw against [Grêmio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grêmio_FBPA "Grêmio FBPA"), the team earned the nickname *Menudos do Morumbi*, in reference to the [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") band [Menudo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menudo_(group) "Menudo (group)").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) Notably, the club also signed the "King of Rome," [Falcão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Roberto_Falcão "Paulo Roberto Falcão"), as the major acquisition of 1985.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) With this team, the club won the [Brazilian Championship in 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1986 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") and the São Paulo State Championships of [1985](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Campeonato_Paulista "1985 Campeonato Paulista") and [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Campeonato_Paulista "1987 Campeonato Paulista").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

In the 1986 Brazilian Championship, São Paulo entered as a favorite, unlike in 1977,[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) but that did not mean an easy path. The early stages went smoothly, with only one defeat. In the knockout rounds, Careca demonstrated a high level of performance: he scored in every match except the first leg against [Fluminense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluminense_Football_Club "Fluminense Football Club"). The club overcame strong opponents and reached the final against [Guarani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guarani_FC "Guarani FC"), Careca’s former team. The first leg ended in a 1–1 draw, with goals from [Evair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evair_Aparecido_Paulino "Evair Aparecido Paulino") for Guarani and Careca for São Paulo—both competition top scorers with 24 goals each. The second leg, played at a packed [Estádio Brinco de Ouro da Princesa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Brinco_de_Ouro_da_Princesa "Estádio Brinco de Ouro da Princesa"), also ended in a 1–1 draw in regulation time, forcing extra time. São Paulo took the lead in the first minute, but Guarani equalized six minutes later. At the five-minute mark of the second half of extra time, Guarani went ahead 3–2, and, confident that there was no time for another equalizer, the stadium’s loudspeaker began playing the club’s anthem. However, with just one minute remaining, the ball fell to Careca, who equalized and took the lead in the scoring charts. Once again, the title was decided on penalties, and again, it went to the *Tricolor do Morumbi*.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The year 1988 was not fruitful in titles and marked the end of the *Menudos* era, but it enriched the club’s assets with the inauguration on April 9 of the Frederico Antonio Germano Menzen Training Center—also known as the CT Barra Funda—in the Barra Funda neighborhood, covering an area of 44,472 square meters.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) It was built to better accommodate the club’s main squad, as the Morumbi Stadium, despite being comfortable, no longer met all the team’s needs with the modernization of the sport.[[39]](#cite_note-siteoficial_ctbarrafunda-39)

The team performed poorly in 1988, even with the signing of [Bobô](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raimundo_Nonato_Tavares_da_Silva "Raimundo Nonato Tavares da Silva"), and achieved little. The year 1989 seemed to follow the same pattern, but with a change in management, renewed motivation for the existing squad—including [Raí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raí "Raí")—and the signing of [Ricardo Rocha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Roberto_Barreto_da_Rocha "Ricardo Roberto Barreto da Rocha"), the team won the [Paulista Championship of 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Campeonato_Paulista "1989 Campeonato Paulista").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

A notable characteristic of this era was that in its five state championship wins, the team always started poorly and recovered as the competition progressed, earning the nickname "*time de chegada*" (team of arrivals). As a result, fans were not concerned with a poor start in championships, confident that the team could still win the title.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

## The Telê era — 1990 to 1994

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Telê era — 1990 to 1994")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Tel%C3%AA_Santana_da_Silva_01.jpg/250px-Tel%C3%AA_Santana_da_Silva_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Telê_Santana_da_Silva_01.jpg)

Telê Santana, the coach who won two World Championships and two Libertadores with São Paulo.

After nearly two decades of success, some predicted a decline for the club, which seemed likely in 1990. In the [Paulista Championship of that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Campeonato_Paulista "1990 Campeonato Paulista"), São Paulo performed poorly, failing to qualify among the sixteen teams advancing to the second phase, which would compete in the stronger group the following year. The team needed a win in the relegation playoff against [Botafogo de Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botafogo_Futebol_Clube_(SP) "Botafogo Futebol Clube (SP)") to maintain title aspirations but managed only a draw, and even a 6–1 thrashing of [Noroeste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esporte_Clube_Noroeste "Esporte Clube Noroeste") in the final round was not enough to secure qualification.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

This episode is among the most contentious in the annals of São Paulo's football history, prompting the inquiry of whether the club would be relegated in 1990. Nonetheless, during the 1988 and 1989 seasons, a system for relegation was not in place.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[40]](#cite_note-placar_1024a-40) The 1990 regulations, following the previous years, did not provide for relegation to the immediately lower division.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[40]](#cite_note-placar_1024a-40)[[41]](#cite_note-blogdobirner_rebaixamento1-41)

> For the 1991 Professional Football First Division Championship, Group I will consist of the 14 associations qualified to compete in the fourth phase of the 1990 Championship, and Group II will consist of the ten remaining associations that did not qualify for the fourth phase, plus four promoted from the 1990 Special Division.

— **Paragraph 1 of Article 5 of the 1990 São Paulo State Championship regulations**, [[41]](#cite_note-blogdobirner_rebaixamento1-41)

> In the 1990 professional football first division championship, there will be no relegation to the professional football special division. However, starting in 1991, or each year thereafter, one association from the First Division will be relegated, and one association from the Special Division will be promoted.

— **Paragraph 2 of Article 5 of the 1990 São Paulo State Championship regulations**, [[41]](#cite_note-blogdobirner_rebaixamento1-41)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Rai_em_2009_cropped_2.jpg/250px-Rai_em_2009_cropped_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rai_em_2009_cropped_2.jpg)

Raí, a key leader in the 1992 Libertadores and World Championship victories.

Returning to the championship, São Paulo, now under [Telê Santana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telê_Santana "Telê Santana"), could not improve its standing in the 1990 Paulista Championship. However, in the [Paulista Championship of 1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Campeonato_Paulista "1991 Campeonato Paulista"), the team improved, taking advantage of matches against weaker opponents to reach the finals and ultimately win the title against Corinthians. The standout player of this championship, and for some time thereafter, was Raí, who joined the club and, despite being instrumental in the 1989 title, was not universally accepted. He was booed and nearly loaned out, but Telê’s insistence paid off, as Raí led the club to another state title.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Telê turned the team around, as after two consecutive final losses, they won the [Brazilian Championship in 1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "1991 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), becoming three-time champions.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Subsequently, the potential to accomplish any objective was apparent,[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) so much so that in 1992, the club prioritized winning the [1992 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Copa_Libertadores "1992 Copa Libertadores"). In the [Libertadores of 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Copa_Libertadores "1972 Copa Libertadores"), São Paulo had been one draw away from the final; in [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Copa_Libertadores "1974 Copa Libertadores"), they lost the final in a playoff match; and in [1978](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Copa_Libertadores "1978 Copa Libertadores"), [1982](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Copa_Libertadores "1982 Copa Libertadores"), and [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Copa_Libertadores "1987 Copa Libertadores"), they did not advance past the first phase. The trophy was a priority for the club, but not for Telê, who considered the competition unfair. Thus, he fielded only three starters in the opening match and lost 3–0 to [Criciúma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criciúma_Esporte_Clube "Criciúma Esporte Clube"). However, the board insisted and pushed the coach to prioritize the South American competition, noting that it would now include [anti-doping tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_sport "Doping in sport"), a request that was promptly met.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) The team improved throughout the competition. In the first leg of the final in [Buenos Aires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buenos_Aires "Buenos Aires"), [Newell’s Old Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newell's_Old_Boys "Newell's Old Boys") won 1–0. In the return leg, an unprecedented scene unfolded: hours before the match, the Morumbi Stadium was already full, with 105,185 people inside and another 15,000 outside—and fans kept arriving. The access roads to the stadium were clogged. Driven by a packed stadium, the Libertadores title was finally won on penalties after a 1–0 victory in regulation time. The fans invaded the pitch to celebrate in a party São Paulo had never seen before.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

With this title, the club faced an even greater challenge: taking on [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Barcelona "FC Barcelona") led by [Johan Cruyff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johan_Cruyff "Johan Cruyff")—considered the best Barcelona of all time[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)—featuring stars such as [Koeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Koeman "Ronald Koeman"), [Stoichkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hristo_Stoichkov "Hristo Stoichkov"), and [Laudrup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Laudrup "Michael Laudrup") in the [Intercontinental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Intercontinental_Cup "1992 Intercontinental Cup"). Earlier, in August, São Paulo had already defeated the same Barcelona 4–1 in the [Teresa Herrera Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Herrera_Trophy "Teresa Herrera Trophy"). In the World Championship match, Barcelona took the lead, but two goals from Raí turned the game around, giving the title to Telê Santana’s team. São Paulo was finally the best team in the world. Upon their return, São Paulo prevailed over another team in the second leg of the [Paulista Championship of 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Campeonato_Paulista "1992 Campeonato Paulista") final: Palmeiras, which was enduring a 16-year title drought.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Armelino_Donizetti_Quagliato_%28Zetti%29_02.jpg/250px-Armelino_Donizetti_Quagliato_%28Zetti%29_02.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Armelino_Donizetti_Quagliato_(Zetti)_02.jpg)

Zetti, the starting goalkeeper for the 1992 and 1993 titles.

> São Paulo was impeccable throughout the entire match. They won with complete fairness.

— Johan Cruyff, Barcelona’s coach after the defeat to São Paulo in the 1992 Intercontinental Cup, [[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

> If you’re going to be run over, it’s better to be hit by a Ferrari.

— Johan Cruyff, [[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)[[42]](#cite_note-42)

After reaching the top of the world, São Paulo needed to stay there. To that end, the [Libertadores of 1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Copa_Libertadores "1993 Copa Libertadores") was again given top priority, with the advantage that, as the 1992 champions, the team entered directly into the knockout phase. The squad was well-prepared, with peak technical and tactical performance, ready for a year in which they would play 97 matches.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

São Paulo advanced more easily through their opponents compared to the previous year and reached the finals against [Universidad Católica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Deportivo_Universidad_Católica "Club Deportivo Universidad Católica") from [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"). In the first leg at Morumbi, they delivered a resounding 5–1 thrashing, virtually securing the trophy. The Chilean club's 2–0 victory in the second leg did not diminish the significance of the triumph, which set a new record for the largest margin of victory in a Libertadores final. This was Raí’s last championship with the club before he moved to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

São Paulo narrowly missed a Libertadores/Paulista double. The club was knocked out of the finals against Palmeiras due to a loss to Corinthians, in which [Neto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Ferreira_Neto "José Ferreira Neto") scored a clearly offside goal, and a legitimate goal by [Palhinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Ferreira_da_Silva "Jorge Ferreira da Silva") was disallowed.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) In the [Recopa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Recopa_Sudamericana "1993 Recopa Sudamericana"), the club won its first title, defeating [Cruzeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruzeiro_Esporte_Clube "Cruzeiro Esporte Clube") on penalties, and two months later, they won the [Supercopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_Supercopa_Libertadores "1993 Supercopa Libertadores") against [Flamengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Jorge_Ferreira_da_Silva_%28Palhinha%29_01.jpg/250px-Jorge_Ferreira_da_Silva_%28Palhinha%29_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jorge_Ferreira_da_Silva_(Palhinha)_01.jpg)

Palhinha, the club’s top scorer in the 1993 Libertadores.

São Paulo reached the Intercontinental Cup final again, this time against [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan") led by [Fabio Capello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabio_Capello "Fabio Capello"), the only [Italian champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Football_Championship "Italian Football Championship") to go unbeaten in history. The match was highly anticipated, as experts considered both teams the best in the world at the time.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Milan dominated early, pressuring São Paulo and creating the best chances to score, but it was São Paulo who took the lead. The Italians equalized in the second half from a corner kick, but eleven minutes later, São Paulo regained the lead. At the 36th minute, Milan tied the game again. It seemed extra time was inevitable, and the Brazilian team might lack the stamina after nearly a hundred matches that year. However, Müller was fortunate in this instance: following a move initiated by [Toninho Cerezo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toninho_Cerezo "Toninho Cerezo"), the ball deflected off the Italian goalkeeper, struck Müller's heel, and then rolled into the net: 3–2.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) São Paulo's victory was achieved through counter-attacks, thereby securing their second world title.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

> Last year, the superteam was Barcelona, but we came to Tokyo and beat them. This year, the superteam was Milan. And we beat them too. So I ask: if they are superteams, what is São Paulo, then? I’d like someone to answer that…

— [Ronaldão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronaldo_Rodrigues_de_Jesus "Ronaldo Rodrigues de Jesus"), [[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

São Paulo reached the finals of the [Libertadores in 1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Copa_Libertadores "1994 Copa Libertadores") but could not secure the third title. Much of 1994 was unsuccessful, with the exceptions of the [Recopa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Recopa_Sudamericana "1994 Recopa Sudamericana"), won against [Botafogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botafogo_de_Futebol_e_Regatas "Botafogo de Futebol e Regatas"), and the [Copa CONMEBOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_CONMEBOL "Copa CONMEBOL"). Notably, the club’s surprise that year was the so-called "*Expressinho*,"[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) the youth and reserve team that played friendly matches and tournaments when the main squad was unavailable. This team, featuring young talents such as[Rogério Ceni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Ceni "Rogério Ceni"), [Juninho Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osvaldo_Giroldo_Júnior "Osvaldo Giroldo Júnior"), and [Denílson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denílson_de_Oliveira_Araújo "Denílson de Oliveira Araújo"), was tasked with competing in, among other tournaments, the [Copa CONMEBOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Copa_CONMEBOL "1994 Copa CONMEBOL") (a precursor to the current [Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sudamericana "Copa Sudamericana")), and won the title, defeating [Peñarol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Peñarol "Club Atlético Peñarol") with a 6–1 thrashing in the first leg of the final.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Telê Santana stayed with São Paulo for five years. During this period, he won every possible competition for a Paulista club (except the Copa do Brasil): the São Paulo State Championship, Brazilian Championship, Libertadores, Copa CONMEBOL, Supercopa Libertadores, Recopa Libertadores, Intercontinental Cup, and the [Ramón de Carranza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramón_de_Carranza_Trophy "Ramón de Carranza Trophy") and [Teresa Herrera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Herrera_Trophy "Teresa Herrera Trophy") tournaments.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

In 1993, the club decided to organize and showcase its achievements. After ten months of planning, the Luiz Cássio dos Santos Werneck Memorial was inaugurated in 1994.[[43]](#cite_note-siteoficial_memorial-43) The name honors Luiz Cássio dos Santos Werneck, a loyal supporter of Cícero Pompeu de Toledo during the construction of the Morumbi Stadium.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Until then, the club’s history had not been meticulously preserved, and São Paulo was a pioneer in this type of initiative.[[43]](#cite_note-siteoficial_memorial-43)

The memorial was established to display not only on-field achievements but also off-field accomplishments. It also aims to highlight significant moments in the club’s history and the broader sports world. The memorial houses the trophies won throughout the club’s history, personal items of Éder Jofre, Leônidas da Silva, and Adhemar Ferreira da Silva, portraits of players and idols, the history of the Morumbi Stadium, and the achievements of all sports practiced by the club.[[43]](#cite_note-siteoficial_memorial-43)

## 1995 to 2004

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: 1995 to 2004")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Ricardo_Izecson_dos_Santos_Leite_%28Kak%C3%A1%29_01.jpg/250px-Ricardo_Izecson_dos_Santos_Leite_%28Kak%C3%A1%29_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ricardo_Izecson_dos_Santos_Leite_(Kaká)_01.jpg)

Kaká, a São Paulo youth product and the world’s best player in 2007.

In 1995, Telê Santana fell ill and stepped away until 1996, when he was permanently replaced: the "Telê Era" was over.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) Compounding this, a structural renovation of the stadium to install dampers sidelined football.[[44]](#cite_note-folha_29299_vacasmagras-44) The team was regarded as lacking in maturity, and three runner-up finishes in 1996/97—two state championships and a Supercopa—earned it the nickname "*viceado*".[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Between 1995 and 2004, fourteen coaches passed through the club, with no major titles won during this period.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

The team had talented players, including Rogério Ceni, [França](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Françoaldo_Sena_de_Souza "Françoaldo Sena de Souza"), and [Denílson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denílson_de_Oliveira_Araújo "Denílson de Oliveira Araújo"), and signed [Gallo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Gallo "Alexandre Gallo"), [Capitão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleúde_José_Ribeiro "Oleúde José Ribeiro"), and [Márcio Santos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Márcio_Roberto_dos_Santos "Márcio Roberto dos Santos"). With this squad, the club reached the finals of the [Paulista Championship of 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Campeonato_Paulista "1998 Campeonato Paulista"). It was with Raí’s return, solely for the final, that the club won its 19th state title.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Raí had agreed to return since 1997, with the transfer set to be finalized in May 1998. However, as Raí was already in São Paulo and planned to attend the final, a club director consulted the São Paulo Football Federation to confirm his eligibility and received approval. All documentation was rushed to ensure he could play legally. The players unanimously accepted his return and made room for him in the lineup. The move paid off, as with Raí on the field, São Paulo defeated Corinthians 3–1, with Raí scoring a goal and providing an assist.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

The following year started poorly, with three consecutive semifinal eliminations. The team needed to make squad changes and switch coaches to pursue the desired titles. In 2000, the team won the [Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Campeonato_Paulista "2000 Campeonato Paulista") in a final that marked Raí’s last title with São Paulo. With this victory, the Tricolor ended the century as the most successful team in São Paulo state championships on average, with one title every 3.33 seasons, compared to 3.91 for Corinthians and 4.09 for Palmeiras.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Until that year, the club had not won two titles: the [Rio-São Paulo Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio-São_Paulo_Tournament "Rio-São Paulo Tournament") and the [Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_do_Brasil "Copa do Brasil"). They lost the [Copa do Brasil of 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Copa_do_Brasil "2000 Copa do Brasil") final, where they needed only a draw with goals against [Cruzeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruzeiro_Esporte_Clube "Cruzeiro Esporte Clube") but suffered a 2–1 comeback loss at the 44th minute of the second half.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) Shortly after the elimination, Raí retired definitively from football.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

The Rio-São Paulo Tournament was always cherished by fans, and by 2001, São Paulo had competed in 21 editions, with runner-up finishes as their best results in 1933, 1962, 1965, and 1998. Whenever the team was poised to win, something prevented their triumph. In 1949, São Paulo was set to face Corinthians in the final, needing only a draw, but the match was postponed due to the [Copa América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_América "Copa América") and never took place. In 1956, the club won the national phase of the competition, but it was not official, as all Rio de Janeiro teams withdrew.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

However, in 2001, without Raí but with [Luís Fabiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Fabiano_Clemente "Luís Fabiano Clemente"), [Júlio Baptista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Júlio_César_Baptista "Júlio César Baptista"), and [Kaká](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaká "Kaká"), São Paulo reached the Rio-São Paulo final and defeated [Botafogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botafogo_de_Futebol_e_Regatas "Botafogo de Futebol e Regatas").[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

Some time later, in July 2001, the team was without one of its greatest idols, [Rogério Ceni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Ceni "Rogério Ceni"), for nearly a month, accused by the board of fabricating an offer from [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_F.C. "Arsenal F.C.") in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"). With the help of several staff, teammates, and even directors, he managed to overcome the situation. During this period, the current club idol was nearly transferred to Cruzeiro, which backed out at the last minute.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45) By this time, the team already had the experience of [Leonardo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonardo_Nascimento_de_Araújo "Leonardo Nascimento de Araújo"), who had returned from Italy.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)

In 2002, São Paulo had a disastrous year: they lost another Rio-São Paulo final to Corinthians, were eliminated from the Copa do Brasil by the same team, and in the Brazilian Championship, they were knocked out after two losses to the Santos team led by [Robinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robson_de_Souza "Robson de Souza").[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) The sole redeeming factor was the [Supercampeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercampeonato_Paulista "Supercampeonato Paulista"), a tournament featuring the [Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Campeonato_Paulista "2002 Campeonato Paulista") champion, [Ituano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ituano_FC "Ituano FC"), and the top three São Paulo teams from that year’s Rio-São Paulo, the last edition of the tournament.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

In boxing, the club managed to have the era’s greatest boxer wear São Paulo’s colors. On August 3, 2002, boxer [Acelino Freitas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acelino_Freitas "Acelino Freitas"), known as Popó, defeated [Daniel Attah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Attah "Daniel Attah") by points in [Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), representing São Paulo. There was an attempt to hold one of his fights at the Morumbi Stadium, but it was unsuccessful.[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47)

In 2003 and 2004, the most the club achieved was qualification for the Libertadores, a competition they had not participated in for ten years.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) Otherwise, the team went through this period with a financial crisis,[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6) a focus on the stadium over football,[[44]](#cite_note-folha_29299_vacasmagras-44) tactically unbalanced squads, and roster changes.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45) In 2003, with his image already tarnished among fans, Kaká left the club after a short stint.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) In 2004, São Paulo lost in the semifinals to [Once Caldas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Once_Caldas "Once Caldas") from [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") and was eliminated from the [Libertadores of 2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Copa_Libertadores "2004 Copa Libertadores"). Upon returning to Brazil, they went straight to [Belém](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belém "Belém"), where they lost to [Paysandu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paysandu_Sport_Club "Paysandu Sport Club"). Back in the capital, they were greeted with stones from fans,[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7) and during the classic against Palmeiras, the crowd chanted "*pipoqueiros*" (chokers) while wearing yellow shirts. The team’s spirit needed to change.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45) In the latter part of the year, Luís Fabiano departed from the club, leaving it devoid of idols. At the time, Rogério Ceni was regarded as a highly skilled goalkeeper but not as an idol.[[7]](#cite_note-alexandre_almanaque-7)
