In 2004, the club also inaugurated the Sports, Physiotherapy, and Physiological Rehabilitation Center, REFFIS, to treat club employees and athletes, as well as those from other organizations.[[39]](#cite_note-siteoficial_ctbarrafunda-39) It is regarded as the most contemporary facility of its kind owned by a club in South America and is regarded as a model in Brazil.[[39]](#cite_note-siteoficial_ctbarrafunda-39)[[48]](#cite_note-48)

## 2005 to 2008

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2005 to 2008")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Sao_paulo_e_atletico_paranaense_-_copa_libertadores_de_2005_-_01.jpg/250px-Sao_paulo_e_atletico_paranaense_-_copa_libertadores_de_2005_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sao_paulo_e_atletico_paranaense_-_copa_libertadores_de_2005_-_01.jpg)

Electronic scoreboard showing the result of the 2005 Libertadores final.

The team already had a solid foundation, and with the signings of [Mineiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Luciano_da_Silva "Carlos Luciano da Silva"), [Josué](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josué_Anunciado_de_Oliveira "Josué Anunciado de Oliveira"), and [Luizão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Carlos_Bombonato_Goulart "Luiz Carlos Bombonato Goulart"), it was complete for its priority: the [Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Copa_Libertadores "2005 Copa Libertadores"). Under [Emerson Leão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerson_Leão "Emerson Leão")’s command, the team adopted a warrior’s spirit and won the [Paulista Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Campeonato_Paulista "2005 Campeonato Paulista") with ease. However, Leão unexpectedly resigned after the title, in the middle of the Libertadores. [Paulo Autuori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Autuori "Paulo Autuori") took over, continuing and even improving the previous work. Under his leadership, the team breezed through all South American opponents until reaching the final against [Atlético Paranaense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlético_Paranaense "Atlético Paranaense"), the first final contested between clubs from the same country.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8e/Mineiro.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mineiro.jpg)

Mineiro, scorer of the goal in the 2005 World Championship.

In the first leg, played at [Estádio Beira-Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Beira-Rio "Estádio Beira-Rio") due to the [Arena da Baixada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Joaquim_Américo_Guimarães "Estádio Joaquim Américo Guimarães")’s insufficient capacity of 40,000, São Paulo secured a 1–1 draw, leaving the decision for the Morumbi. On July 14, 2005, São Paulo won the title for the third time. The second leg was much easier, with São Paulo dominating from the start and opening the scoring in the first half. In the second half, they achieved a decisive 4-0 victory, the second-largest margin in Libertadores final history, becoming the first Brazilian team to win the competition three times.[[6]](#cite_note-giacomini_dentre-6)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/SPFC_squad_-_2005_-_01.jpg/250px-SPFC_squad_-_2005_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPFC_squad_-_2005_-_01.jpg)

Tribute received from the São Paulo Football Federation and President [Lula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Inácio_Lula_da_Silva "Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva") for the third world championship.

Once again, the team set out for the [world title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_FIFA_Club_World_Championship "2005 FIFA Club World Championship"), this time in a tournament fully organized by FIFA. The first opponent was [Al-Ittihad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ittihad_Club_(Jeddah) "Al-Ittihad Club (Jeddah)"). There was fear among the squad of a major upset, and the media reported a rift in the team over the "bonus" issue, which never occurred.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45)

After a few hours, the expected opponent was confirmed: [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C."), with São Paulo as the underdog. The English team’s goalkeeper had not conceded a goal in eleven matches.[[49]](#cite_note-placar_mundial2005-49) Rogério Ceni, already a club idol, played the final with an injured finger and a [medial meniscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medial_meniscus "Medial meniscus") issue.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45) In a fast-paced match, Liverpool pressured São Paulo with aerial balls and long passes, while the Tricolor played a defensively perfect game and scored a goal.[[49]](#cite_note-placar_mundial2005-49) Thus, the team secured a 1–0 victory with Mineiro’s goal, Rogério’s saves, and the team’s grit and determination.[[45]](#cite_note-rogerio_maioridade-45) The three-time champion team exhibited a warrior-like spirit and valiant determination, though it lacked the talent of the 1992 and 1993 teams. However, it demonstrated a comparable level of deservingness, as it achieved victory in the championship with greater ease compared to the 1992 squad.[[49]](#cite_note-placar_mundial2005-49)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Sao_paulo_e_juventude_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2006_-_01.jpg/250px-Sao_paulo_e_juventude_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2006_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sao_paulo_e_juventude_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2006_-_01.jpg)

The Brazilian Championship match against Juventude drew one of the largest crowds of the tournament.

After the title, a dismantling of the champion team was inevitable. Few key players were lost, one of the most significant being full-back [Cicinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicinho "Cicinho"), but he was adequately replaced by [Ilsinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilsinho "Ilsinho"). The team remained under the leadership of Rogério Ceni, now coached by [Muricy Ramalho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muricy_Ramalho "Muricy Ramalho"). After runner-up finishes in the [Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Campeonato_Paulista "2006 Campeonato Paulista"), [Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Copa_Libertadores "2006 Copa Libertadores"), and [Recopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Recopa_Sudamericana "2006 Recopa Sudamericana"), the team made the [Brazilian Championship of 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2006 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") their priority and only salvation for the season. The team led the table for nearly the entire championship, had the best attack and defense, and finished nine points ahead of the runner-up. The title-clinching match, as in previous championships, was a draw, this time 1–1 against Atlético Paranaense in the third-to-last round. The campaign’s highlights were Rogério Ceni, who led the team, won the championship missing from his collection, and became the [world’s highest-scoring goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_goalscoring_goalkeepers "List of goalscoring goalkeepers"), and the fans, who filled the Morumbi Stadium. With the 2006 Brazilian Championship, São Paulo maintained its tradition of winning a Brazilian title every decade.[[50]](#cite_note-lance_brasileiro2006-50)

On October 18, 2006, the city of São Paulo enacted law number 14,229, dated October 11 of the same year, based on bill number 648 of 2005, establishing December 16 as "Tricolor Day" to commemorate the club’s refounding date.[[51]](#cite_note-projetolei_648_2005-51)[[52]](#cite_note-lei_14229_2006-52)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Choque_rei_-_palmeiras_e_sao_paulo_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2007_-_01.jpg/250px-Choque_rei_-_palmeiras_e_sao_paulo_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2007_-_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Choque_rei_-_palmeiras_e_sao_paulo_-_campeonato_brasileiro_de_2007_-_01.jpg)

A *[Choque-Rei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choque-Rei "Choque-Rei")* match that ended with a 1–0 Tricolor victory.

In 2007, the team lost key players again and was eliminated early in the [Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Campeonato_Paulista "2007 Campeonato Paulista") and [Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Copa_Libertadores "2007 Copa Libertadores"). Once again, Muricy faced pressure to leave, but thanks to president [Juvenal Juvêncio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal_Juvêncio "Juvenal Juvêncio"), he stayed. The start of the [Brazilian Championship of 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2007 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") was shaky, partly due to the Libertadores elimination, but the Tricolor gained momentum and led the table by the end of the first half. Their winning streak was so strong that they went 16 games without a loss, including 14 victories. They also went 688 minutes without conceding a goal in the tournament over nine matches. São Paulo revealed new talents, such as [Hernanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernanes "Hernanes") and [Breno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breno_(footballer,_born_1989) "Breno (footballer, born 1989)"). The title-clinching match had a different flavor, secured with a victory. The club needed only a draw against [América](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/América_FC_(RN) "América FC (RN)") from [Rio Grande do Norte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Grande_do_Norte "Rio Grande do Norte"), but they won 3–0. With this title, despite the year’s turbulence, coach Muricy Ramalho entered history as one of the few two-time Brazilian Championship-winning coaches.[[53]](#cite_note-lance_brasileiro2007-53)

That same year, the club began implementing a project for an area in the [Morumbi Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_do_Morumbi "Estádio do Morumbi"), called *Morumbi Concept Hall*, aimed at increasing foot traffic, strengthening the club’s brand, and boosting revenue on non-match days, thus expanding entertainment, business, and leisure options for São Paulo residents and tourists.[[54]](#cite_note-54)

As a first step in this venture, the club launched the *Rbk Concept Store*, inaugurated on August 27, 2007. Spanning 700 square meters, the megastore is the largest of its kind in a stadium in Latin America and includes a VIP box for match days.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Rogerio_ceni.jpg/250px-Rogerio_ceni.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rogerio_ceni.jpg)

[Rogério Ceni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Ceni "Rogério Ceni"), leader of the three-time world champion and six-time Brazilian champion team.

The year passed, and 2008 unfolded similarly to the previous year: the team was eliminated in the [Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Campeonato_Paulista "2008 Campeonato Paulista") and [Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Copa_Libertadores "2008 Copa Libertadores"), leaving the [Brazilian Championship of 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2008 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") as their chance for redemption. The problem was that the team took a long time to find its rhythm, and at the start of the second half, the leader [Grêmio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grêmio_FBPA "Grêmio FBPA") had an 11-point lead over the Tricolor. However, as the season progressed, the team made a strategic decision to pursue another title, marking the first three-peat in the club's history. They achieved a decisive victory over all direct competitors, maintaining an unblemished record for 16 consecutive games. The 2008 team reflected Muricy's coaching style, yet Rogério Ceni was, once again, the team's leader.[[56]](#cite_note-placar_brasileiro2008-56)

The final match, this time, took place in the last round against [Goiás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goiás_Esporte_Clube "Goiás Esporte Clube") during a turbulent moment. Just before the decisive match, where a draw would suffice for São Paulo, Marco Pólo Del Nero, president of the FPF, advised by a GAECO prosecutor, contacted the [CBF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Football_Confederation "Brazilian Football Confederation") president [Ricardo Teixeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Teixeira "Ricardo Teixeira"), alleging that an envelope addressed to the match referee, Wagner Tardelli, had been sent by São Paulo as an attempt to bribe him.[[57]](#cite_note-justicadesportiva_madonna1-57)

Upon learning of this, the Arbitration Committee, through a new draw to protect the referee’s and championship’s integrity, replaced the referee for the decisive match. An inquiry was launched by the STJD to identify those responsible. On February 13 of the following year, after reviewing the case, the [CBF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Football_Confederation "Brazilian Football Confederation"), the referee, and São Paulo were cleared of bribery charges due to lack of evidence, and a new inquiry was opened to investigate the conduct of the federation and its president.[[57]](#cite_note-justicadesportiva_madonna1-57) On March 4, the FPF was fined ten thousand [reais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_real "Brazilian real"), and the president was suspended for ninety days for filing an unfounded complaint.[[58]](#cite_note-justicadesportiva_madonna2-58)

Thus, although everything was clarified later, the match was played amid significant off-field controversy, but the players remained focused on the decisive game. The title-clinching goal came from the offside [Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humberlito_Borges_Teixeira "Humberlito Borges Teixeira"), a 1–0 victory in a match that would have secured the title for the *Tricolor do Morumbi* even without the goal. With this win, the club achieved an unprecedented three-peat in the Brazilian Championship and secured their sixth title.[[56]](#cite_note-placar_brasileiro2008-56)

## Difficult years — 2009 to 2020

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Difficult years — 2009 to 2020")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Majestoso_-_sao_paulo_and_corinthians_-_campeonato_paulista_of_2009_-_03.jpg/250px-Majestoso_-_sao_paulo_and_corinthians_-_campeonato_paulista_of_2009_-_03.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Majestoso_-_sao_paulo_and_corinthians_-_campeonato_paulista_of_2009_-_03.jpg)

São Paulo fans celebrating despite the loss to [Corinthians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_Club_Corinthians_Paulista "Sport Club Corinthians Paulista") in the Paulista semifinal.

The new year began with high hopes that the team would have an exceptional season and finally win the [2009 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Copa_Libertadores "2009 Copa Libertadores"), as the team had failed three times in a row, and each time it was a Brazilian team that defeated them. The squad was kept intact and new players were brought in, creating a sense of optimism for the year.[[59]](#cite_note-placar_libertadores2009-59)

The [2009 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Campeonato_Paulista "2009 Campeonato Paulista") was initially given secondary importance, as the Libertadores was the primary target. The club even considered fielding a reserve team in some matches, but this idea was quickly discarded.[[60]](#cite_note-60) Nevertheless, the club managed only a fourth-place finish in the state competition.[[61]](#cite_note-61) Focused on the Libertadores, the club also underperformed and was eliminated in the quarter-finals by another Brazilian team, this time [Cruzeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruzeiro_EC "Cruzeiro EC").[[62]](#cite_note-62) [Muricy Ramalho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muricy_Ramalho "Muricy Ramalho")'s departure occurred due to the conclusion of a significant cycle at the club, where he had previously secured three consecutive Brazilian championships. However, the team had encountered challenges in the most crucial competition, the Libertadores.[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64)

Following Muricy's dismissal on 19 June,[[65]](#cite_note-65) [Ricardo Gomes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Gomes_Raymundo "Ricardo Gomes Raymundo") was hired the following day after talks began the previous night.[[66]](#cite_note-66) In the match the following day against Corinthians, [Milton Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Cruz "Milton Cruz") took charge of the team on an interim basis[[67]](#cite_note-67) and the new coach was officially presented on Wednesday.[[68]](#cite_note-68) After the change in management, the team gained momentum in the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2009 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") and climbed from 14th position to the top four — the group of teams qualifying for the Libertadores — with a chance even to win a fourth consecutive championship, which would have been the seventh national title in its history.[[69]](#cite_note-69) However, after stumbles in the final stretch of the competition, the club finished in third place. As a consolation, they secured their seventh consecutive participation in the Libertadores, the 15th in their history, making them the Brazilian club with the most appearances in the competition.[[70]](#cite_note-70)

The 2010 season began with high expectations for the São Paulo fans, with the board bringing in [Fernandinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luiz_Fernando_Pereira_da_Silva "Luiz Fernando Pereira da Silva"), a revelation from the 2009 Campeonato Brasileiro with [Grêmio Barueri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grêmio_Barueri_Futebol "Grêmio Barueri Futebol"),[[71]](#cite_note-71) and players such as [Cicinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicinho "Cicinho"),[[72]](#cite_note-72) [Alex Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Sandro_da_Silva "Alex Sandro da Silva"),[[73]](#cite_note-73) and [Marcelinho Paraíba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelinho_Paraíba "Marcelinho Paraíba").[[74]](#cite_note-74) However, the year was not successful for São Paulo. After a decent campaign in the [2010 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Campeonato_Paulista "2010 Campeonato Paulista"), where they were eliminated by Santos led by [Neymar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neymar "Neymar"), [Paulo Henrique Ganso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Henrique_Ganso "Paulo Henrique Ganso"), and [Robinho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinho "Robinho"),[[75]](#cite_note-75) the team focused solely on the Copa Libertadores. After finishing as the second-best team in the group stage, behind rivals Corinthians, São Paulo eliminated [Universitario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Universitario_de_Deportes "Club Universitario de Deportes") from [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru") on penalties after two 0-0 draws.[[76]](#cite_note-76) Next, they faced their previous Libertadores nemesis, Cruzeiro, now reinforced with [Fernandão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernandão_(footballer,_born_1978) "Fernandão (footballer, born 1978)"), a long-time target of the board, who debuted with a 2-0 victory at [Mineirão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineirão "Mineirão"), a result repeated in the return leg at [Morumbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_do_Morumbi "Estádio do Morumbi"),[[77]](#cite_note-77) advancing to the semifinals after three years to face another Brazilian team, [Internacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SC_Internacional "SC Internacional"). The semifinals, however, were played after the [2010 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup"). During this period, Cicinho returned to [Roma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AS_Roma "AS Roma"), and Washington, the club's top scorer in the Libertadores, went back to [Fluminense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluminense_FC "Fluminense FC"), but another former player, [Ricardo Oliveira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Oliveira "Ricardo Oliveira"), returned. São Paulo lost the first leg at [Beira-Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beira-Rio "Beira-Rio") 1-0 with a poor performance and won the return leg 2-1, but were eliminated due to the away goals rule. This marked their fifth consecutive Libertadores elimination by a Brazilian club, sealing Ricardo Gomes' dismissal.[[78]](#cite_note-78)

In the Brasileirão, São Paulo had a steady start due to their focus on the Libertadores. After Gomes' departure, the board promoted [Sérgio Baresi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sérgio_Baresi "Sérgio Baresi") to head coach. He had won the [Copa São Paulo de Futebol Júnior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_São_Paulo_de_Futebol_Júnior "Copa São Paulo de Futebol Júnior") earlier that year and knew the youth players but lacked experience.[[79]](#cite_note-79) Poor results forced his exit after fourteen games. His positive contribution was the promotion of young talents such as [Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Rodrigues_Moura_da_Silva "Lucas Rodrigues Moura da Silva") and [Casemiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Henrique_Casemiro "Carlos Henrique Casemiro") to the main squad. [Paulo César Carpegiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_César_Carpegiani "Paulo César Carpegiani"), who was performing well with [Atlético-PR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Athletico_Paranaense "Club Athletico Paranaense"), was hired in his place.[[80]](#cite_note-80) Despite aiming to qualify for the 2011 Libertadores, he was unsuccessful: São Paulo finished only ninth and missed the Libertadores for the first time in eight years.[[81]](#cite_note-81)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/JSP_0799.JPG/250px-JSP_0799.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:JSP_0799.JPG)

Luís Fabiano, one of the recent idols of the São Paulo fans.

The 2011 season was the worst in many years for São Paulo: the team was eliminated from the [2011 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Campeonato_Paulista "2011 Campeonato Paulista") by Santos again,[[82]](#cite_note-82) from the Copa do Brasil by [Avaí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avaí_Futebol_Clube "Avaí Futebol Clube") (which was relegated to Série B that same year),[[83]](#cite_note-83) and from the [2011 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Copa_Sudamericana "2011 Copa Sudamericana") by [Libertad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Libertad "Club Libertad") from Paraguay.[[84]](#cite_note-84) In the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2011 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), São Paulo finished in sixth place, one position short of qualifying for the Libertadores. However, not everything was negative for São Paulo in 2011. That year, goalkeeper [Rogério Ceni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Ceni "Rogério Ceni") scored his 100th career goal in a victory over Corinthians in the Paulistão, breaking an eleven-game winless streak against their rivals. Additionally, the goalkeeper also played his 1,000th match for São Paulo against [Atlético Mineiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Mineiro "Clube Atlético Mineiro") in the Campeonato Brasileiro.[[85]](#cite_note-85) The board also announced the signing of [Luís Fabiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Fabiano "Luís Fabiano") for 7.6 million euros, the most expensive acquisition in São Paulo’s history at the time, in March, although the striker only returned to the pitch in October due to a knee injury sustained while still playing for [Sevilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevilla_FC "Sevilla FC").[[86]](#cite_note-86)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Lucas_Moura.jpg/250px-Lucas_Moura.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lucas_Moura.jpg)

Lucas Moura, a player sold for 108 million reais.

Attempting to erase the negative impression left by the previous year’s team, accused of lacking grit, São Paulo went on a spending spree and signed several players for the 2012 season, including [Paulo Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Miranda_(footballer,_born_1988) "Paulo Miranda (footballer, born 1988)"), [Jádson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jádson "Jádson"), [Fabrício](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrício_de_Souza "Fabrício de Souza"), [Bruno Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Cortez "Bruno Cortez"), and [Osvaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osvaldo_(footballer,_born_1987) "Osvaldo (footballer, born 1987)"),[[87]](#cite_note-87) while continuing to back the work of coach [Émerson Leão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Émerson_Leão "Émerson Leão"), hired in the final stretch of the 2011 Brasileirão. The results were unsatisfactory: the team started well in pursuit of the [2012 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Campeonato_Paulista "2012 Campeonato Paulista"), but could not withstand Santos and was eliminated by them for the third consecutive time in the semifinal, in a match where defender Paulo Miranda (already heavily criticized for repeated errors) fell out of favor with the fans.[[88]](#cite_note-88) This episode marked his sidelining from the club, which was aiming for the unprecedented conquest of the [2012 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Copa_do_Brasil "2012 Copa do Brasil"). The team advanced past [Ponte Preta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associação_Atlética_Ponte_Preta "Associação Atlética Ponte Preta") and [Goiás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goiás_Esporte_Clube "Goiás Esporte Clube") but fell in the semifinal against [Coritiba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coritiba_Foot_Ball_Club "Coritiba Foot Ball Club").[[89]](#cite_note-89) After the elimination, protests similar to those in 2004 (after the elimination against [Once Caldas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Once_Caldas "Once Caldas") in the Libertadores) began among the fans. Leão was sacked shortly afterward, and [Milton Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Cruz "Milton Cruz") took over again as interim coach, with [Ney Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ney_Franco "Ney Franco") hired for the remainder of the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2012 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"). During this period, São Paulo fans witnessed the successes of their biggest rivals (Santos won the Paulista title for the third time,[[90]](#cite_note-90) [Palmeiras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") won the [2012 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Copa_do_Brasil "2012 Copa do Brasil"), ending a drought of over ten years without major titles,[[91]](#cite_note-91) and [Corinthians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_Club_Corinthians_Paulista "Sport Club Corinthians Paulista") won their first [Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Copa_Libertadores "2012 Copa Libertadores")).[[92]](#cite_note-92) Mid-season, the São Paulo board announced the sale of midfielder [Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Rodrigues_Moura_da_Silva "Lucas Rodrigues Moura da Silva") to [Paris Saint-Germain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Saint-Germain_FC "Paris Saint-Germain FC") for 108 million reais, the largest transfer fee for a Brazilian club at the time—though the player would only join the French club in January 2013.[[93]](#cite_note-93)

Under Ney Franco, São Paulo recovered in the season and finished the [Brasileirão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2012 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") in fourth place, securing the long-awaited return to the [2013 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Copa_Libertadores "2013 Copa Libertadores") after two years of absence.[[94]](#cite_note-94) During the season, the club also announced the signing of [Paulo Henrique Ganso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Henrique_Ganso "Paulo Henrique Ganso"), in the largest transaction between two Brazilian clubs in history.[[95]](#cite_note-95) Additionally, São Paulo set attendance records at the [Morumbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Cícero_Pompeu_de_Toledo "Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo"), achieving the highest crowds in the Brasileirão and CONMEBOL competitions that season, which was capped off with the controversial, unbeaten, and unprecedented conquest of the [2012 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Copa_Sudamericana "2012 Copa Sudamericana"). During the competition, São Paulo eliminated [Bahia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esporte_Clube_Bahia "Esporte Clube Bahia"), faced [Liga de Loja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liga_de_Loja "Liga de Loja"), and defeated the [2011 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Copa_Sudamericana "2011 Copa Sudamericana") champion, [Universidad de Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Universidad_de_Chile "Club Universidad de Chile"), with a resounding 5-0 victory in the return leg. In the semifinal, they defeated [Universidad Católica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Deportivo_Universidad_Católica "Club Deportivo Universidad Católica") and set up a final against [Tigre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Tigre "Club Atlético Tigre") from [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"). In the first leg of the final, São Paulo held on for a 0-0 draw despite facing significant challenges, including the expulsion of [Luís Fabiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Fabiano "Luís Fabiano"). In the second leg, São Paulo scored 2-0 in the first half with goals from [Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Rodrigues_Moura_da_Silva "Lucas Rodrigues Moura da Silva") and [Osvaldo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osvaldo_(footballer,_born_1987) "Osvaldo (footballer, born 1987)"), in a match marked by rough play from the Argentines. At halftime, Lucas showed a blood-soaked piece of cotton, the result of an elbow from [Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Orbán "Lucas Orbán") of Tigre. This sparked a widespread brawl that led to the expulsion of [Paulo Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Miranda_(footballer,_born_1988) "Paulo Miranda (footballer, born 1988)") from São Paulo and Días from Tigre. The Argentine club refused to return to the field for the second half after a locker room altercation. As a result, the Chilean referee [Enrique Osses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Osses "Enrique Osses") ended the match, and São Paulo claimed the unprecedented title, their 12th international title and 41st official title, ending a four-year title drought.[[96]](#cite_note-96)

For the 2013 season, with six competitions ahead (Campeonato Paulista, Copa Libertadores, Campeonato Brasileiro, Copa Sudamericana, and also the [Suruga Bank Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J.League_Cup_/_Copa_Sudamericana_Championship "J.League Cup / Copa Sudamericana Championship") and Recopa Sudamericana), São Paulo secured the signing of experienced defender [Lúcio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucimar_da_Silva_Ferreira "Lucimar da Silva Ferreira") and brought in one of the revelations of the previous Brasileirão, striker [Aloísio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aloísio_dos_Santos_Gonçalves "Aloísio dos Santos Gonçalves"), along with [Negueba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negueba "Negueba"), [Wallyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallyson "Wallyson"), and the return of full-back [Thiago Carleto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiago_Carleto "Thiago Carleto").[[97]](#cite_note-97)

In the [Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Campeonato_Paulista "2013 Campeonato Paulista"), São Paulo again finished the first phase in first place. In the quarter-finals, they eliminated [Penapolense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Penapolense "Clube Atlético Penapolense"), in a match marked by the use of a commemorative all-red jersey. However, in the semifinal, they succumbed to rivals Corinthians on penalties at home: São Paulo had not beaten their rivals at [Morumbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Cícero_Pompeu_de_Toledo "Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo") since 2007.[[98]](#cite_note-98) In the [2013 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Copa_Libertadores "2013 Copa Libertadores"), São Paulo advanced past [Bolívar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Bolívar "Club Bolívar") in the first phase with an 8-5 aggregate score. In the group stage, they struggled, failing to win any away games, but a 2-0 victory at Morumbi against [Atlético Mineiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Mineiro "Clube Atlético Mineiro"), combined with [The Strongest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strongest "The Strongest")’s loss to [Arsenal de Sarandí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_de_Sarandí "Arsenal de Sarandí"), secured their place in the round of 16, preventing what would have been the worst participation in the club’s history in the international competition. They then faced Atlético again in the knockout stage and were defeated, once again by a Brazilian team, with a 4-1 thrashing in the return leg.[[99]](#cite_note-99)

This elimination led to the sidelining of seven reserve players from the squad. The board clashed with striker [Luís Fabiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luís_Fabiano "Luís Fabiano") after statements from president [Juvenal Juvêncio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal_Juvêncio "Juvenal Juvêncio"),[[100]](#cite_note-100) but kept coach [Ney Franco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ney_Franco "Ney Franco") in place despite protests from some fans. The team signed some reinforcements from smaller Paulista clubs for the rest of the season and confirmed participation in two additional competitions that year, the [Audi Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audi_Cup "Audi Cup") and the [Eusébio Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusébio_Cup "Eusébio Cup"), both played in Europe, where São Paulo would tour during the second half of the year.[[101]](#cite_note-:0-101)

The return after the break was disastrous. São Paulo lost the [Recopa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recopa_Sudamericana "Recopa Sudamericana") to rivals Corinthians with two defeats and suffered the worst streak of results in the club’s history, with eight consecutive losses and eleven games without a win. Ney Franco was sacked during the Recopa, and [Paulo Autuori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulo_Autuori "Paulo Autuori"), the coach who won the Libertadores and Club World Cup with the club eight years earlier, was hired.[[102]](#cite_note-102) The experienced [Clemente Rodríguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemente_Rodríguez "Clemente Rodríguez") was the only reinforcement in the international transfer window.[[103]](#cite_note-103)

On their European tour, São Paulo held off [Bayern Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Bayern_Munich "FC Bayern Munich") for 55 minutes in the [2013 Audi Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Audi_Cup "2013 Audi Cup") debut until [Mandžukić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Mandžukić "Mario Mandžukić") opened the scoring, and the team ended up losing 2-0. In the third-place match against [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Milan "AC Milan"), they also lost 1-0. In the 2013 Eusébio Cup, São Paulo broke a fourteen-game winless streak, winning 2-0 and claiming the trophy, presented by [Eusébio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusébio "Eusébio") himself. In Japan, for the [2013 Suruga Bank Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Suruga_Bank_Championship "2013 Suruga Bank Championship"), São Paulo finished as runners-up, losing 3-2 to [Kashima Antlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashima_Antlers "Kashima Antlers"), with three goals from [Osako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuya_Osako "Yuya Osako"), one in the final minute.[[101]](#cite_note-:0-101)

The 2014 season started poorly, with an elimination in the [Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Campeonato_Paulista "2014 Campeonato Paulista") quarter-finals on penalties against [Penapolense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Penapolense "Clube Atlético Penapolense"), considered the weakest team among those qualified for the knockout stage.[[104]](#cite_note-104) The poor form continued in the [2014 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Copa_do_Brasil "2014 Copa do Brasil"), with a third-round elimination against [Bragantino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Bragantino "Clube Atlético Bragantino"),[[105]](#cite_note-105) but São Paulo managed to recover and finished the season as [Campeonato Brasileiro runners-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2014 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A").[[106]](#cite_note-106)

In 2015, São Paulo had a strong first phase in the [Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Campeonato_Paulista "2015 Campeonato Paulista") but was again eliminated in the semifinal by Santos, a fate repeated in November in the [2015 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Copa_do_Brasil "2015 Copa do Brasil"). In the [2015 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Copa_Libertadores "2015 Copa Libertadores"), they were knocked out by Cruzeiro in the round of 16 on penalties. In the second half of the year, they had an inconsistent campaign in the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2015 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), amid a political crisis that culminated in the resignation of president [Carlos Miguel Aidar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Miguel_Aidar "Carlos Miguel Aidar") due to corruption allegations,[[107]](#cite_note-107) but managed to secure a spot in the preliminary rounds of the [2016 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Copa_Libertadores "2016 Copa Libertadores"). [Carlos Augusto de Barros e Silva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Augusto_de_Barros_e_Silva "Carlos Augusto de Barros e Silva"), known as Leco, was elected to complete Aidar’s term and was later re-elected in 2017.[[108]](#cite_note-108)

After securing a place in the group stage of the continental competition in two matches against [César Vallejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Deportivo_Universidad_César_Vallejo "Club Deportivo Universidad César Vallejo"), São Paulo started poorly, losing to [The Strongest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Strongest "The Strongest") at Pacaembu and drawing with [River Plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_River_Plate "Club Atlético River Plate") and [Trujillanos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trujillanos_FC "Trujillanos FC") away. A recovery came with two victories at Morumbi against these opponents, allowing São Paulo to play for a draw in La Paz against The Strongest. A 1-1 result secured their place in the round of 16. In the knockout stages, São Paulo eliminated [Toluca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportivo_Toluca_F.C. "Deportivo Toluca F.C.") and [Atlético Mineiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_Atlético_Mineiro "Clube Atlético Mineiro") before facing [Atlético Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlético_Nacional "Atlético Nacional") in the semifinals. In two matches marred by poor refereeing, São Paulo was eliminated.[[109]](#cite_note-109)[[110]](#cite_note-110)

In the [Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Campeonato_Paulista "2016 Campeonato Paulista"), the club had an inconsistent campaign and had to play a single quarter-final match in Osasco against [Audax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grêmio_Osasco_Audax "Grêmio Osasco Audax"), where they were thrashed 4-1. The [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2016 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A") campaign was even worse, with the club spending much of the championship in the bottom half of the table and finishing in tenth place. Mid-season, the board had to replace Argentine coach [Edgardo Bauza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgardo_Bauza "Edgardo Bauza"), who left to manage the [Argentina national football team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina_national_football_team "Argentina national football team"), with Ricardo Gomes. Under the shadow of Rogério Ceni, who was considered to take over as coach,[[111]](#cite_note-111) Gomes was sacked in November.[[112]](#cite_note-sombra_de_Ceni-112) A few days later, the former goalkeeper was announced as the coach for 2017.[[112]](#cite_note-sombra_de_Ceni-112)

Rogério’s debut as coach started with a team that scored many goals but also conceded many.[[113]](#cite_note-113) While the coach tried to fix this issue, the team was eliminated in less than a month in the semifinals of the [Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Campeonato_Paulista "2017 Campeonato Paulista"), the round of 32 of the [2017 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Copa_do_Brasil "2017 Copa do Brasil"), and the first phase of the [2017 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Copa_Sudamericana "2017 Copa Sudamericana") by [Defensa y Justicia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensa_y_Justicia "Defensa y Justicia"), who were making their international competition debut.[[114]](#cite_note-114) With a terrible start in the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2017 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), the board could not withstand the pressure and sacked Rogério, with the team in the relegation zone. His replacement, [Dorival Júnior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorival_Júnior "Dorival Júnior"), received reinforcements such as [Hernanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernanes "Hernanes") and led the team to one of the best second-half campaigns, but could not escape a modest 13th-place finish.[[115]](#cite_note-115)

However, following a defeat to Palmeiras in the [2018 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Campeonato_Paulista "2018 Campeonato Paulista"), Dorival was dismissed from his position.[[116]](#cite_note-116) His replacement, [Diego Aguirre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Aguirre "Diego Aguirre"), reached the semifinal of the same tournament and came close to eliminating Corinthians, but a late goal led to a penalty shootout, ending the dream of breaking the state title drought that year. For the second consecutive year, São Paulo failed to reach the round of 16 of the [2018 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Copa_do_Brasil "2018 Copa do Brasil") (eliminated by [Atlético Paranaense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Athletico_Paranaense "Club Athletico Paranaense"))[[117]](#cite_note-117) and was knocked out by [Colón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Colón "Club Atlético Colón") in the [2018 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Copa_Sudamericana "2018 Copa Sudamericana").[[118]](#cite_note-118)

In the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2018 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), the team had its best first-half campaign, winning the symbolic title, but injuries and dips in form from some players exposed a squad with few alternatives, unable to maintain the same pace in the second half of the season.[[119]](#cite_note-119) Besides losing the title, São Paulo also lost a direct spot in the group stage of the [2019 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Copa_Libertadores "2019 Copa Libertadores"), finishing in a frustrating fifth place. Aguirre was sacked with five rounds to go, with the board trying to maintain at least fourth place under interim coach [André Jardine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/André_Jardine "André Jardine"), but the change did not yield the desired results.

With Jardine confirmed as head coach at the start of 2019, São Paulo began the Libertadores preliminary round against [Talleres de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Talleres "Club Atlético Talleres"), losing in Argentina and failing to overturn the result at Morumbi, drawing 0-0 and being eliminated in the preliminary phase. As the [Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Campeonato_Paulista "2019 Campeonato Paulista") campaign was also poor, Jardine was sacked.[[120]](#cite_note-120) The board hired [Cuca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuca_(footballer,_born_1963) "Cuca (footballer, born 1963)") to replace him, but had to wait nearly two months while the coach recovered from health issues. During this period, [Vagner Mancini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagner_Mancini "Vagner Mancini") took over, managing to qualify for the Paulista knockout stage in the final round. After eliminating [Ituano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ituano_FC "Ituano FC"), São Paulo faced the favored Palmeiras in the semifinal. After two goalless draws, the spot was decided on penalties, and São Paulo prevailed, reaching their first Campeonato Paulista final since [2003 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Campeonato_Paulista "2003 Campeonato Paulista"). With another late goal in the return leg against Corinthians, the team had to settle for the runner-up position.[[121]](#cite_note-121)

Throughout the year, the team struggled to score goals, recording its worst offensive output in history.[[122]](#cite_note-122) This was evident not only in the goalless Libertadores elimination but also in the round of 16 exit in the [2019 Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Copa_do_Brasil "2019 Copa do Brasil") against [Bahia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esporte_Clube_Bahia "Esporte Clube Bahia"), with two 1-0 losses. Despite having the eighth-worst attack in the [Campeonato Brasileiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Campeonato_Brasileiro_Série_A "2018 Campeonato Brasileiro Série A"), São Paulo secured a spot in the group stage of the [2020 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_Libertadores "2020 Copa Libertadores"), thanks to the titles won by Flamengo and Athletico Paranaense in the Libertadores and Copa do Brasil, respectively, which opened two additional spots in the Brasileiro. However, the result did not come under Cuca, who resigned in September, being replaced by [Fernando Diniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Diniz "Fernando Diniz").[[123]](#cite_note-123)

The 2019 balance sheet closed with a deficit of over 150 million reais, raising concerns about the club’s financial health, a situation later worsened by the [COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Brazil "COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil") in 2020, which halted competitions in March. Upon the return of competitions, São Paulo's participation in the Campeonato Paulista came to an end with a 3-2 defeat at the hands of [Mirassol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirassol_Futebol_Clube "Mirassol Futebol Clube") at Morumbi in the semifinal round, fell in the group stage of the [2020 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Copa_Libertadores "2020 Copa Libertadores")[[124]](#cite_note-124) finishing third in their group, and consequently entered the Copa Sudamericana directly against [Lanús](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Lanús "Club Atlético Lanús"). With a 3-2 loss in the first leg in Argentina and a 4-3 win at Morumbi, with the Argentine team scoring in the final seconds, São Paulo was eliminated again, this time due to the away goals rule. In national competitions, the club led the Campeonato Brasileiro for a few rounds but could not maintain the advantage, finishing fourth and also being eliminated in the Copa do Brasil semifinals by [Grêmio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grêmio_Foot-Ball_Porto_Alegrense "Grêmio Foot-Ball Porto Alegrense").[[125]](#cite_note-125)

## End of the title drought, Copa do Brasil title, and "Champion of Everything" — 2021 to 2024

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_FC&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: End of the title drought, Copa do Brasil title, and ")]

After several years of failure, the club returned to winning titles by clinching the [2021 Campeonato Paulista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Campeonato_Paulista "2021 Campeonato Paulista") when they defeated rivals Palmeiras 2-0 in the final at the Morumbi stadium on 23 May 2021. The following year, the club reached two championship finals: the Campeonato Paulista and the Copa Sudamericana, but lost both, with the state final lost to Palmeiras and the continental final to [Independiente del Valle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independiente_del_Valle "Independiente del Valle"). After these two setbacks, the club strove to win its first [Copa do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Copa_do_Brasil "2023 Copa do Brasil") in 2023, putting together an impressive campaign by eliminating their two biggest rivals, defeating Palmeiras in the quarter-finals and Corinthians in the semifinals, before winning the title against Flamengo with a 1-0 victory at Maracanã and a 1-1 draw at Morumbi.[[126]](#cite_note-126)

On 4 February 2024, São Paulo faced rivals Palmeiras at [Mineirão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mineirão "Mineirão") for the [2024 Supercopa Rei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Supercopa_Rei "2024 Supercopa Rei"). The match ended 0-0 in normal time and went to penalties. The *Tricolor Paulista* won 4-2 on penalties and claimed the Supercopa for the first time.[[127]](#cite_note-127) São Paulo became the first and only Brazilian club to win every possible title when they won the Supercopa.[[128]](#cite_note-128)

# São Paulo Futebol Clube

O São Paulo Futebol Clube foi criado a partir da fusão entre o Clube Atlético Paulistano e a Associação Atlética das Palmeiras, em 1930.

O início da história do São Paulo Futebol Clube (SPFC) se deu em função da história do Clube Atlético Paulistano. Este sempre foi um clube de peso na cidade de São Paulo, mas não era a favor do profissionalismo que o futebol estava adotando. O resultado foi que alguns jogadores do Paulistano migraram para um outro clube, a Associação Atlética das Palmeiras, que possuía um estádio próprio, mas que estava com muitas dívidas. Foi essa fusão que deu origem ao São Paulo, no dia 27 de janeiro de 1930, mas, por motivo simbólico (data de aniversário da fundação da cidade de São Paulo), o documento oficial ficou datado de 15 de janeiro de 1930.

Com muitos títulos conquistados desde a primeira década de sua existência, o São Paulo Futebol Clube, na década de 1960, passou a investir na construção de um estádio até hoje gigantesco: o Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, popularmente chamado de Morumbi.

So Paulo is a very traditional Brazilian football team from So Paulo, founded on January 25, 1930, and Re-founded on December 16, 1935. Often called Tricolor by its supporters.

The team is one of the most successful teams in Brazil, with several titles of national and interational grade. That includes two Club's World Championship (Toyota cup).

Home stadium is the Ccero Pompeu de Toledo (aka Morumbi), capacity 80,000. They play in a white shirt with two horizontal stripes--one red and one black, white shorts and socks.

# História do São Paulo: títulos, ídolos e jogos - Terra

O São Paulo Futebol Clube foi fundado em 25 de janeiro de 1930 como São Paulo da Floresta. Após breve período de inatividade, foi refundado em 16 de dezembro de 1935 com o nome atual. É o único time brasileiro que tem três títulos continentais e três mundiais, além de ser o único a conquistar o Campeonato Brasileiro três vezes consecutivas. Duas das estrelas do emblema são-paulino, as douradas, têm relação com outro esporte. Elas representam os recordes mundiais e olímpicos de salto triplo de Adhemar Ferreira da Silva, atleta do clube. Um dos maiores ídolos da história do São Paulo não entrava em campo: Telê Santana foi o comandante da equipe bicampeã mundial.

mais sobre o são paulo

**Nome:** São Paulo Futebol Clube

**Alcunhas:** Tricolor Paulista, Clube da Fé, O Mais Querido, Tricolor do Morumbi

**Fundação:** 16 de dezembro de 1935

**Localização:** São Paulo - SP, Brasil

**Estádio:** Morumbi

**Capacidade:** 67.428

**Presidente:** Juvenal Juvêncio

##### Titular

1° uniforme

##### Reserva

2° uniforme

O Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, conhecido como Morumbi, é o maior estádio particular do Brasil, terceiro maior no geral - atrás de Maracanã e Mineirão. Tem capacidade para 67.428 espectadores, mas chegou a abrigar 146.082 pessoas na final do Campeonato Paulista de 1977, entre Corinthians e Ponte Preta. Até a construção do Morumbi, o São Paulo jogou em outros estádios da cidade, como a Chácara da Floresta, o Pacaembu e o Canindé. O local havia sido escolhido como a sede paulistana para a Copa do Mundo de 2014. No entanto, problemas de logística com o local fizeram a CBF mudar de escolha.

# São Paulo FC

As an inaugural member of Clube dos 13, it’s no surprise that São Paulo Futebol Clube is considered one of the marquee clubs in Brazilian football. Their trophy room speaks for itself: 6 Brasileirão titles, 3 Copa Libertadores trophies, and 21 state titles. Unsurprisingly, they’re also one of the most popular clubs in the country, with more than 16 million fans and an annual revenue of over $100 million.

### Basic facts

Founded: 1930  
 Country: Brazil  
 City: São Paulo

### Home grounds

Chácara da Floresta (1930–1959)  
 Estádio do Morumbi (1960–)

### Main trophies

Campeonato Paulista: 21  
 Brasileiro Série A: 6  
 Copa do Brasil: 5  
 Copa Libertadores: 3

### Prominent players

Leônidas da Silva, Gérson Darío Pereyra, Müller, Leonardo, Raí, Cafu, Rivaldo, Adriano, Kaká, Luís Fabiano

### Club records

Most games played: Rogério Ceni (575)  
 Top goalscorer: Luís Fabiano (56)

![São Paulo Futebol Clube in 1930 line-up in 1930](../images/sao_paulo_1930.jpg)  
 São Paulo Futebol Clube squad in 1930.

## History

### Foundation and early exploits

São Paulo’s official history begins in 1930, when the club was founded by 60 players, former officials, friends, and members of two older clubs from the area: CA Paulistano and AA das Palmeiras. Due to various internal disagreements and financial issues, the club was disbanded in 1935. The same year, it was reformed under the name São Paulo Futebol Clube.

The 40’s were the first truly successful era for São Paulo, which started acquiring star players from competing clubs. The new players settled in fairly quickly, leading the club to five Paulista championship titles by the end of the decade. During this time, the club earned the nickname “The Steamroller.” However, the rise of Pelé’s [Santos](santos.html) in the 50’s soon relegated São Paulo back to the sidelines.   
   
 In 1960, the construction of Estádio do Morumbi, officially named Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo, was finished. This was a huge stadium planned for 120,000 people. The construction of the stadium continued during the decade and it got even more seats - in the end of the decade it was big enough to held an attendance of 140,000! After later reconstructions, the attendance potential has decreased radically.

![Estádio Cícero Pompeu de Toledo black and white](../images/estadio_do_morumbi.jpg)  
 The mighty Estádio do Morumbi in 1970. 

### The Telê era

Despite winning two Brasileirão titles in 1977 and 1986, São Paulo struggled to assert its dominance for most of the 20th century. However, this changed with the arrival of Telê Santana, a respected manager most known for putting together the legendary 1982 and 1986 Brazil national squads. Telê ended up staying at the club for five seasons, and this is widely considered to be one of the most successful periods in the history of São Paulo.

![São Paulo Futebol Clube in 1930 line-up in 1971](../images/sao_paulo_1971.jpg)  
 The team lined up in 1971. 

Led by Telê and the influential midfielder Raí, the club claimed its third Brasileirão title in 1991. The next season, they went one step further and won their first Copa Libertadores title by defeating Newell’s Old Boys in a penalty shoot-out. In 1993, they managed to retain their title by defeating Universidad Católica 5-1 in the first leg of the final; the second leg was merely a formality. Unfortunately, Telê was soon forced to leave the club due to health issues.

### Return to prominence

From 1995 to 2004, São Paulo changed no less than 14 managers. Despite these setbacks, the club remained competitive at the highest level, mainly due to the star power of players such as Kaká, Luis Fabiano, and Rogério Ceni. In 2005, the club finally won its third Copa Libertadores by outlasting Atlético Paranaense in the final. With this victory, São Paulo became the first Brazilian club to claim three Copa Libertadores titles.

In 2006, the controversial Muricy Ramalho took over as coach, immediately implementing his trademark defensive style. Though some of the club’s fans didn’t like this change, they couldn’t argue with the results. From 2006 to 2009, São Paulo won three consecutive Brasileirão titles, with Ramalho becoming the first coach to achieve this feat with the same team.

By Martin Wahl
